POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 22:39:51 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.12 Macron accuses ‘arrogant’ Le Pen of speaking as if she already won https://www.politico.eu/article/macron-accuses-arrogant-marine-le-pen-criticism-eu-budget-negotiations/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 22:39:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9400185 BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron thinks Marine Le Pen should learn to know her place.

Macron on Thursday rejected criticism from the far-right presidential candidate, who is accusing him and EU institutions of deliberately rushing negotiations over the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget to make sure she doesn’t have a say in them.

“Ms. Le Pen is campaigning just like other candidates. It is a strange kind of arrogance to think that she is already in charge of France’s destiny because, until proven otherwise, she has not been elected, and yours truly is elected until May 13, 2027. ” Macron told reporters.

Macron urged more “humility” from Le Pen, stressing that she is not in office yet.

While he hopes that EU leaders can reach a budget deal soon, the French president has warned that, if negotiations are not wrapped up by the end of the year, he will stop participating and leave that task to his successor — which may be Le Pen.

“After December 31, I will not be in a position — from a political or democratic standpoint—to reopen a discussion on the budget and bring it to a conclusion. We will be entering a period that is far too close to the presidential election in France,” he said on Thursday.

Macron already had the same reaction when, in 2024, Le Pen claimed that Macron should refrain from picking the next French EU commissioner during a parliamentary election campaign.

On Thursday evening, the French President appeared extremely disappointed by the direction negotiations were taking and by cuts proposed by the European Council President António Costa and pushed by frugal countries.

“Europe is making a strategic mistake,” he warned.

]]> en Trump diverges from NATO statement, emphasizing Ukraine mustn’t expand war https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-trump-diverges-from-nato-statement-emphasizing-ukraine-mustnt-expand-war/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:40:59 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9398190 BRUSSELS — Donald Trump sprung a surprise on NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte after the two met in Florida amid the U.S. president’s latest push to end the war between Ukraine and Russia.

Following the Wednesday night meeting at Mar-a-Lago, the two leaders said they had “discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible” in a joint statement shared by both the White House and NATO.

Writing hours later on Truth Social, the president altered the tone of the remark by adding two words — changing the statement to say “Russia and Ukraine” must avoid such actions.

A NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive issue, said the original missive was the officially agreed statement between the two sides — signaling Trump had later amended the statement unilaterally.

The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment from POLITICO.

The addition is pointed, coming days after Ukraine struck a Russian warship in a Libyan port, thousands of kilometers from Kyiv. The attack, which legal experts say may have broken international law, has drawn no criticism from most of Ukraine’s allies given Russia’s daily bombardment against its neighbor.

It also highlights persistent tensions between Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian leader who has refused to abandon Kyiv’s long-range strikes against Russian refineries and critical infrastructure. Trump last month said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new President” — blaming Zelenskyy for holding up a peace deal.

That posture marks a contrast to Trump’s recent overtures toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he referred to as a “friend” during last week’s trilateral meeting with the Kremlin boss and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Russian strikes have, for years, continuously targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The updated language also throws up a fresh challenge for Rutte. The former Dutch prime minister has repeatedly lavished praise on the American president in public as he scrambles to maintain U.S. arms shipments and limited support for Ukraine, and unity inside NATO. But the divergence showcases how his approach to keep Trump on message has clear limits.

Despite the Truth Social addition pointing to Ukraine, Trump later added he had “spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe” during the meeting.

Attention will now turn to a NATO foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Dec. 2, which allies had previously expected to line up with a long-anticipated U.S. review of its troop presence in Europe. The U.S. has since told allies the revamp would be delayed.

The Trump-Rutte meeting was originally intended to center around the overhaul, dubbed the Europe Posture Review, the NATO official said, but instead focused on transatlantic defense industrial scale-up and Russian hybrid attacks in Europe as the review’s publication was postponed.

Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report.

]]> fr UK to get ‘Swiss-style’ consultative rights under new EU deals https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-to-get-swiss-style-consultative-rights-under-new-eu-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:06:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9398409 LONDON — Britain will be granted “Swiss-style” consultation rights over European Union legislation but no decision-making powers under agrifood and emissions trading deals agreed at last week’s U.K.-EU summit.

The details were set out in legal texts published on Thursday ahead of the introduction to parliament of the government’s ‘Cutting Costs’ (European Partnership) Bill, the legislation being used to implement the agreements.

The agrifood deal will see the U.K. align with most EU sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) rules, removing the need for costly border controls. The emissions trading system (ETS) deal will reconnect U.K. and EU carbon markets, shielding businesses on both sides from paying carbon taxes.  

Both deals allow the U.K. to be consulted on relevant EU legislative proposals and to contribute views during the drafting process, including through expert discussions and committee meetings. However, the U.K. will have no vote or formal role in EU decision-making.

French negotiators had initially resisted the consultative powers set out in the deals, before ultimately backing down on the eve of the summit. 

Joël Reland, a senior research fellow at UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said the U.K.’s role would be akin to Switzerland, which can participate in early legislative consultation phases and still has to actively apply legislation itself.

This will give parliament “some notional power to resist,” Reland explained, “though with the size of Labour’s majority we’re unlikely to see any obstruction in the near future.”

This model diverges from that of the Windsor Framework, a U.K.-EU deal that controls the flow of goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, where Northern Ireland has no say over the legislation, which is applied by default.

While the U.K. will not be afforded all the rights of an EU member country, Adam Berman, director of policy and advocacy at Energy UK, said it was “positive to see an openness to the U.K. as a decision-shaper” in the ETS deal.

“This should benefit both sides given that the U.K. has substantial expertise in this area,” he added.

Carveout confirmation

In the case of the agrifood deal, the legal text confirms exceptions to alignment on the export of live animals, pet smuggling and precision-bred plants, as well as transitional arrangements for novel foods, pesticides and organic products. These details were set out in an explanatory document published by the U.K. government last week. 

The legal text also confirms reports of a 10-year termination clause in the agrifood deal, which requires either side to pay “reasonable and proportionate” costs to rebuild border infrastructure if the deal is scrapped.

Meanwhile, the text of the ETS deal confirms that the U.K. will have freedom to use its Emissions Trading System to reward high-emitting industries which integrate greenhouse gas removal technologies into their manufacturing processes. 

The U.K. will keep all revenue drawn from its emissions trading scheme and retain autonomy over how it is spent.

The U.K. will be required to pay both an “operational contribution” towards the EU’s food security system, as well as an additional “participation fee,” calculated at 4% of the operational contribution.

]]> en Sweden’s Kristersson edges closer to new term as prime minister https://www.politico.eu/article/sweden-kristersson-edges-closer-new-term-prime-minister/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:11:18 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9397665 Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is closing in on a coalition deal to return for another term as head of government, according to three people aware of coalition talks.

The center-right leader, whose party came in second place in September elections, has struck a deal on a political platform with three other parties in view of forming a government, according to the party officials and diplomats.

The Swedish parliament will vote on Kristersson’s potential reappointment as prime minister on Monday.

“Hour by hour we are getting closer to an EPP-led government in Sweden. On Monday the Parliament will vote and hopefully approve Ulf Kristersson as PM,” said Tomás Tobé, European People’s Party vice chair in the European Parliament and party colleague of Kristersson.

Kristersson’s coalition would not have a majority in parliament and would rely on support from other parties to pass legislation. The far-right Sweden Democrats party previously backed Kristersson’s government but has not said it would support him this time.

A crucial factor is whether the Center Party decides to join the coalition. Previously, the party has resisted joining out of opposition to cooperation with the Sweden Democrats.

“The Center Party is on the verge of abandoning what was arguably its most important and powerful election promise: never to enable the Sweden Democrats to wield political influence,” said a Swedish party official aware of the talks. They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to discuss the sensitive negotiations.

Following reports that the Center Party has taken a preliminary decision to join a four-way coalition government, Kristersson said “there was no alternative to a minority government … it won’t be easy but it isn’t always easy to be in government.”

Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson won the election in September but has since failed to reach a parliamentary majority. Andersson’s failed attempts at forming a government dealt a heavy blow to the EU’s Socialists, which after Sunday’s election in Spain could also lose Pedro Sánchez to a right-wing coalition.

That would leave them with two out of 27 leaders — Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Malta’s Robert Abela.

Swedish parties have been negotiating for 73 days to form a government following an election in September. 

This article has been updated with comments from Kristersson.

]]> en EU Commission offers little in response to US drug pricing pressures https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-commission-offers-little-in-response-to-us-drug-pricing-pressures/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:58:49 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9395721 EU lawmakers hoping for a stronger response from the European Commission to U.S. pressure on capitals to raise drug prices got little in the way of new commitments on Thursday.

Addressing the European Parliament plenary for the first time on the matter, Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen said there were “too many uncertainties” to assess the impact of Washington’s drug pricing push on Europe.

The Trump administration has been pressuring European countries to pay more for new medicines, arguing that American citizens disproportionately shoulder the cost of pharmaceutical innovation through higher drug prices.

In response to the Trump administration’s use of trade measures to push countries to raise drug prices, she also said European industry was protected by last year’s transatlantic trade truce struck at President Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf resort in Scotland. The subsequent joint statement that put the deal in writing set a 15% tariff ceiling on most European exports to the U.S., including branded medicines.

Berlin faces possible additional tariffs after Washington launched a Section 301 investigation in June into Germany’s alleged “persistent underpayment” for innovative pharmaceuticals. Washington’s aim is to strike a deal to raise drug prices, similar to an agreement signed with the U.K.

“We have to have a coordinated response,” European People’s Party MEP Tomislav Sokol told the debate in Strasbourg. Bilateral deals “would weaken the European position.”

Some EU countries — including France and Ireland — recently asked the Commission to set up a task force bringing together national trade and health officials to assess the U.S. demands and explore a joint response.

Renew MEP Stine Bosse, who initiated the plenary debate, warned that other capitals could find themselves in Washington’s crosshairs. “Today it is Germany,” she said. “Member states must work closer together than ever before on joint clinical assessment and yes, on pricing and reimbursement.”

Drug pricing is a sensitive national matter, while trade policy falls within the EU’s remit.

Belgium’s Deputy Prime Minister and Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke recently published a paper arguing that the Commission should consider deploying its Anti-Coercion Instrument — the EU’s trade “bazooka” — in response to U.S. pressure.

Socialist lawmaker Vytenis Andriukaitis and Renew MEP Vlad Vasile Voiculescu backed consideration of the instrument. Virkkunen, however, did not address that option.

Romana Jerković, another socialist, warned that EU legislation such as the Critical Medicines Act would take years to yield benefits. The Trump administration’s policy of tying U.S. drug prices to those paid elsewhere, known as most-favored nation pricing, has prompted pharmaceutical companies to delay medicine launches in Europe.

“What are the projects the Commission is planning to respond to the decline [of medicine launches] in the short term?” Jerković asked.

Virkkunen cited legislation such as the forthcoming Biotech Act and said the Commission “fully respects” national powers over pricing but that “we can also provide support when needed” — without specifying what that support would entail.

She also stressed the need for continued cooperation with Washington. “I believe that there is more that connects us than divides us,” she said.

The topic is expected to come up again when EU health ministers meet on Dec. 8.

]]> en EU leaders clear path for Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos to lead ECB https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-leaders-clear-path-for-spains-pablo-hernandez-de-cos-to-lead-ecb/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:57:34 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9396909 BRUSSELS — Spain has a clear path to the most powerful economic job in Europe after the Netherlands gave up the chase for the presidency of the European Central Bank.

At the EU leaders’ summit, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten agreed to back a political deal that France, Germany and Spain had crafted in recent weeks to decide the ECB’s leadership for years to come.

The Netherlands had initially put forward its former central bank governor, Klaas Knot, for the top job. But the political deal leaves Knot empty-handed.

The deal will see Spain’s own ex-governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, succeed ECB President Christine Lagarde when she steps down on Feb. 7. In return, Germany will appoint Markus Brunnermeier as the ECB’s chief economist, while the markets portfolio on the bank’s six-person executive board will go to France’s Laurence Boone.

The ECB sets interest rates, which dictate borrowing costs across the single-currency bloc, with a mandate to keep inflation steady at 2% over the medium term.

“Based on the conversation today” among EU leaders, “the Netherlands will support the consensus for the three nominations for the ECB board,” an EU diplomat said. Such consensus would be “an important signal to financial markets.”

EU ambassadors have since formally recommended the three candidates for the ECB posts, another EU diplomat said. That will allow EU leaders to kick-start a “consultation process” today with the European Parliament and the ECB, which have the right to give their views on the three candidates.

“The Council texts agreed today recommend Pablo Hernández de Cos as ECB President and Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier to the Executive Board,” the diplomat said.

A hearing in Parliament is scheduled for Dec. 7, followed by a committee vote, which needs to be rubber-stamped in the plenary the week after. Leaders will then formally cement the deal at their next meeting in Brussels on Dec. 17.

]]> en US to delay overhaul of military presence in Europe https://www.politico.eu/article/us-to-delay-overhaul-of-military-presence-in-europe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:53:22 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9395823 BRUSSELS — The U.S. has told NATO allies it will postpone an overhaul of its force presence in Europe beyond a provisional Dec. 1 deadline, according to two NATO diplomats.

At a meeting of NATO envoys on Wednesday, U.S. deputy ambassador Scott Oudkirk told allies Washington would not present the Europe force posture review in time for a meeting of alliance foreign ministers next Wednesday, said the diplomats, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the classified meeting.

The review, announced by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in June, is designed to examine U.S. force levels across Europe, including troop levels, military access, basing rights and overflight permissions, as Washington seeks to pivot its military engagement toward other regions, such as the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific.

“We’re still hopeful to meet the Dec. 1 deadline — at least for [U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth] to have the final review,” U.S. deputy Pentagon chief Elbridge Colby told reporters in Brussels last week, praising “enormous progress” by nations like Germany, Poland, the Netherlands and Scandinavian countries for “stepping up” and spending more on their own defense.

The U.S. did not give a new date for when it would announce the revamp, the diplomats added, but cited the fact that it was still processing allies’ various offers for supplying military capabilities to replace Washington’s existing equipment and forces as one reason behind the delay.

The U.S. delegation to NATO did not respond to a request for comment.

Allies had previously suggested the review might be delayed amid uncertainties around Hegseth’s future in the administration, following an attempt to oust him after the U.S. midterm elections. The closed-door announcement marks the first confirmation that Washington would push back the review.

In recent months, Colby and other U.S. officials have toured countries like Romania, Poland and Germany in preparation for the overhaul. The U.S. currently has around 80,000 troops stationed on the continent, mostly in Germany, Italy and the U.K.

]]> en Europe’s food security starts with resilient farms https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-content/europes-food-security-starts-with-resilient-farms/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=sponsored-content&p=9332712 Growing up in Brittany, France, food was never simply about what was on the plate. My grandparents were farmers, so I grew up understanding the connection between the food we eat, the people who produce it and the land on which we all depend. That connection has stayed with me.

Yet that foundation is under pressure. Climate change, volatile input costs and geopolitical uncertainty are putting growing strain on Europe’s agri-food chain, raising a fundamental question: how do we build a food system capable of withstanding shocks while continuing to provide safe, nutritious and affordable food?

Agriculture depends on assets we cannot replace: healthy soils, water and functioning ecosystems. Protecting and restoring those assets is not simply an environmental benefit. It is an economic and resilience imperative.

And the scale of the challenge is significant. According to Eurostat, the EU is home to 8.8 million farms managing more than 156 million hectares of agricultural land.1 At that scale and diversity, there can be no one-size-fits-all solution.

This is where regenerative agriculture can make a difference. It is an outcome-based approach, adapted to local conditions, that puts soil health at its core and aims to preserve the land’s productive capacity and strengthen farms’ resilience.

But farmers cannot carry the cost and risk of the transition alone. Research published in 2025 found that transitioning to regenerative agriculture can require upfront investments of €2,000-5,000 per hectare, while the business case can take three to five years to turn positive.2

Agriculture depends on assets we cannot replace: healthy soils, water and functioning ecosystems. Protecting and restoring those assets is not simply an environmental benefit. It is an economic and resilience imperative.

Public and private financing must therefore work together to give farmers the confidence to invest for the long term.

At Nestlé, we have already seen what long-term investment can deliver. At a global level, Nestlé sources 6.9 million tons of agricultural raw materials from Europe every year. By 2030, we aim to increase the volume sourced from farms adopting regenerative agriculture practices across key ingredients from 21 percent in 2025 to 50 percent in 2030.

Through initiatives such as our Nestlé Dairy Plan in Europe, and our Cereal & Grains regenerative agriculture programs, we combine financial support, agronomic expertize and digital tools to help farmers adopt and validate regenerative practices.

There is growing evidence that this transition can work economically for farmers. In Spain, dairy farms receiving Nestlé support recorded an 11 percent increase in milk yield following investment. This reflects the impact of the broader program, which combines regenerative agriculture with measures to improve farm efficiency and resilience. Farms applying minimum tillage also reduced diesel use by 41 percent, while farms with covered manure lagoons reduced their share of synthetic fertilizer by 26 percent.

In the UK, our Fresh Milk Plan with dairy cooperative First Milk is already showing encouraging signs. After four years, soil carbon stocks measured on three participating farms showed an average gain of 8.9 tons of carbon per hectare.3

But resilience is about more than productivity and economics. European farmland bird populations have declined by 58 percent since 1980, underlining the pressure on agricultural ecosystems and the need to understand which interventions can make a measurable difference. That is why Nestlé has partnered with BirdLife Europe on a science-led program using farmland birds, butterflies and wild bees as indicators to measure how regenerative agriculture practices can support biodiversity. The aim is to understand what works and focus investment where it can deliver the greatest impact. A five-year study with SEO/BirdLife across Nestlé’s fresh-milk farms in northern Spain recorded 116 bird species, including 25 species in national decline, showing how dairy landscapes can provide vital refuges for biodiversity while continuing to produce food.

Evidence, however, is only part of the equation. To bring regenerative agriculture to scale, the economics must work for farmers. As the post-2027 CAP takes shape, Article 10 should provide a strong framework for Transition Payments that help de-risk the transition and enable public and private funding to work together effectively.

Resilience is a shared responsibility. Farmers, manufacturers, retailers, policymakers and consumers all have a role to play. That requires balanced and fair relationships across the food chain, where every actor has the means to adapt, innovate and invest for the future. A competitive food system must balance affordability today with resilience tomorrow.

On December 2, in Brussels, we will bring these voices together to discuss what is needed to make regenerative agriculture work for farmers and strengthen Europe’s food resilience.

For me, Europe now needs to get three things right.

Resilience is a shared responsibility. Farmers, manufacturers, retailers, policymakers and consumers all have a role to play.

First, put farmer economics at the heart of the transition. Farmers need a viable business case, not simply additional expectations.

Second, align public and private investment behind measurable outcomes. We should reward what works: stronger farm economics, healthier soils, more efficient use of inputs and greater resilience.

Third, protect the ability of every part of the food value chain to invest and commit for the long term. Europe will not strengthen its food security without fairness for all.

Europe cannot have a resilient food system without resilient farms. Healthy land supports stronger farms; stronger farms underpin resilient food supplies. The task now is to move from individual successes to change at scale.

]]> en Mandelson failed to sell shares in company after becoming US ambassador, latest files show https://www.politico.eu/article/peter-mandelson-failed-to-sell-shares-in-company-after-becoming-us-ambassador-latest-files-show/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:35:59 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9395316 LONDON — Peter Mandelson failed to sell his stake in his lobbying firm Global Counsel and attempted to influence No. 10 decisions after becoming ambassador to the U.S., according to a newly released tranche of documents relating to his appointment.

The files, published Thursday, lay bare the civil service’s frantic efforts to smooth the process of his unorthodox recruitment as the U.K.’s envoy to Washington, as well as his attempts to exert influence beyond his official role. Mandelson was sacked in September 2025 over the depth of his past friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The emails show that at the time of his appointment Mandelson retained his shares in Global Counsel and that, despite having received an offer to buy them in March 2025, had failed to divest them six months later. The company collapsed in February 2026 after it lost a series of accounts amid coverage of Mandelson’s relationship with Epstein.

Senior civil servants exchanged emails late into the Christmas period at the end of 2024 and early 2025 discussing propriety questions, with then head of the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office Philip Barton seeking clarity about what arrangements could be made if Mandelson did not immediately sell his shares, such as placing them in a blind trust.

A person with knowledge of Mandelson’s situation said the peer was not asked to divest his shares before taking up the appointment and a blind trust was ruled out by the Foreign Office.

In April 2025, Mandelson emailed a U.S. official to propose a lunch meeting to discuss how to approach trade with China and suggested bringing an unidentified “former trade colleague” who could “lead off” the discussion, specifying: “It would be best to keep this under the radar.”

The person with knowledge of Mandelson’s situation said that his proposal was to invite a Global Counsel former colleague to a trade trade think in — but that it never took place.

While serving as ambassador, Mandelson also said he would water down language relating to China in a speech after receiving feedback from an unnamed director at Global Counsel, the files reveal.

In an email, the director said: “As you will see, I have made suggestions on toning down some parts of your apologia of the Trump administration. Scepticism of it is now so deep — at least in the public policy-interested world outside government — that it would be counterproductive/unpersuasive if you came across as having drunk the Kool-Aid.”

Mandelson also attempted to intervene in a Cabinet reshuffle by then Prime Minister Keir Starmer in September 2025 via texts to Morgan McSweeney, then No. 10 chief of staff. He suggested moving Darren Jones to lead the science and technology department as a way to “solve your Darren issue.”

McSweeney did not respond until the reshuffle had concluded and Jones was given a newly created role as chief secretary to the prime minister.

Starmer — who was replaced as prime minister by Andy Burnham in July —  found his authority severely weakened over accusations he didn’t take enough enough care to ensure Mandelson, a known friend of Epstein, was a suitable person to be U.K. ambassador to the United States. 

A spokesperson for Burnham said that while the appointment had been made under the previous administration, “we are clear nothing like this can ever happen again, which is why we will ensure lessons are learnt.”

During a statement in the House of Commons, Security Minister Dan Jarvis said Mandelson’s appointment had raised questions about the government’s appointments, vetting and conflicts of interest processes and ministers will respond to an Ethics and Integrity Commission lobbying review before the Christmas recess.

Jarvis said further documents have been withheld at the request of the Metropolitan Police, which is currently investigating Mandelson on suspicion of misconduct in public office. Mandelson has not been charged, and his lawyers have said he is cooperating with the investigation and that his overriding priority is to clear his name.

This developing story has been updated.

Isabel Loubser contributed to this report.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 26 Nov 2026 23:51:31 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 EU leaders leave Brussels with no budget deal, piling pressure on Christmas summit https://euobserver.com/252027/eu-leaders-leave-brussels-with-no-budget-deal-piling-pressure-on-christmas-summit/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 23:36:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=252027 The so-called 'frugal' EU states want deeper cuts, the 'Friends of Cohesion' group wants agriculture and regional funding spared, and Antonio Costa's €204bn compromise satisfies no one. ]]> EU leaders failed to reach agreement on the bloc’s next long-term budget at a summit on Thursday night (26 November) in Brussels, where the so-called frugal countries and pro-cohesion camp remained far apart.

Negotiations were based on a new, substantially-reduced, budget compromise that is 10.3 percent, or €204bn in current prices, below the nearly €2 trillion EU Commission proposal for 2028-34.

But a group of net payer countries, led by Germany, wanted further cuts to the budget. 

“It will not remain at €204bn. It will be less,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters late at night. “I have always made my position clear. The reduction compared to the commission proposal must be several hundred billion euros.” 

And Merz then made clear that “in nominal terms, €200bn is at the very bottom end of what can be considered ‘several’,’’ – suggesting he’d like to see substantial further reductions to the size of the budget. 

His French counterpart Emmanuel Macron however described the  €204 billion reduction as a “strategic error”.

“We are effectively setting ourselves up for a decline in European public investment compared to China, and France does not support any additional cuts,” he said as he left the summit early. 

Despite his wish for a larger EU budget, Macron also made clear France would not contribute more to the EU budget. “We all hope to stabilise national contributions. That’s the challenge we have before us,” he said. 

And the French president also rejected Dutch suggestions of reducing the EU’s agriculture fund to free up cash for innovation and competitiveness, saying that France instead wants to postpone repaying Covid-era debt to “give more ambition to the budget, and reduce national contributions”.

Read more

A ‘bad’ summit first, an EU budget deal later

Measuring size 

Not all were unhappy about the size of EU Council president Antonio Costa’s budget proposal, however. Cypriot president Nikos Christodoulides, for his part, called the overall 10-percent cut “a very logical compromise.” 

Measured against the EU’s economic output, Costa’s budget proposal comes in at 1.07 percent of gross national income (GNI), below the 1.12 percent of the current budget agreed in 2020. If Covid-era repayments are subtracted, the budget is even smaller comparatively, at around 0.97 percent of GNI.

That would make the next budget substantially smaller than the current one, which expires at the end of 2027. But net contributing countries, a group that also includes the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland, with Belgium as an ‘associate member’ want nominal size to shrink, and have called on Costa to present another budget with further cuts. 

“He [Costa] really has to, because we cannot afford this,” a senior diplomat of one of the frugal countries said. The biggest disagreement however wasn’t about size of the budget, but about where the axe should fall. 

Everybody knew what not to cut

Phrased differently, everybody had a strong opinion about what not to cut, but almost nobody knew what should or could be cut. 

A large group of 17 ‘Friends of Cohesion’, mostly central, eastern and southern net recipients (those who get more from the budget than they pay in), resisted cuts to agriculture and cohesion.

Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš, one of them, vowed to “fight” for cohesion funds. 

Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker, a member of the frugal squad, also insisted on a smaller budget, but rejected any suggestion to reduce the size of the agriculture budget. 

In a move seen as a negotiation tactic, Germany’s Merz didn’t specifically take aim at any of the envelopes.

The Dutch were the exception and knew exactly where the cuts should be made: in the “old-fashioned policies” of cohesion and agriculture.

]]> A ‘bad’ summit first, an EU budget deal later https://euobserver.com/251964/a-bad-summit-first-a-eu-budget-deal-later/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:49:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251964 Everyone at the summit insists their red lines are unbreakable — yet the real story is how far they will bend once the ticking clock, Ukraine’s bills and looming 2027 elections start to crush their resolve.]]> Budget talks in Brussels are expected to run late on Thursday (26 November) as EU leaders clash over how big the next seven-year budget should be, who foots the bill and whether all 27 must pay for Ukraine – with time running short to reach a deal before the end of the year. 

On the table is a nearly €2 trillion budget for 2028-2034. But no deal was really ever expected to come out of this special European Council. 

In line with an unspoken Brussels tradition, EU Council president António Costa knew he needed a ‘bad’ summit before a ‘good’ one would even be possible. 

At the last EU budget negotiations, the ‘special summit’ in February 2020 failed – without even clarifying next steps.

The real deal only came after a five-day summit five months later in July 2020 – a pattern that could be repeated this December if a deal is achieved then, as Costa hopes (having previously warned that he could stay until Christmas to make the deal happen). 

Costa’s cuts reduce the overall size of the next budget for 2028-2034 by €204bn, compared with the European Commission’s initial proposal.

Notably, new priorities that need financing, such as research or innovation, have received the biggest cuts, alongside development aid, because agriculture and regional funds are politically too important for a majority of EU leaders.  

Read more

Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

EU budgets always come in at a little above one percent of gross national income (GNI), as so-called ‘frugal’ countries (some of those who pay more to the budget than they receive) refuse to go higher.

Costa’s proposal is close at 0.97 percent of GNI, with pandemic recovery debt repayments subtracted. 

‘Cheap’ is an expensive mistake

But many feel the budget is too small.

“Europe is making a strategic mistake,” French president Emmanuel Macron said during a press conference in the middle of the summit.

“A cheap Europe could turn out to be a very expensive mistake. Security comes at a price,” warned Polish prime minister Donald Tusk. 

The budget fight always follows the same steps. The commission usually proposes a high budget, EU leaders demand huge cuts, the European Parliament then object to the cuts, and then falls in line after making some small gains. 

MEPs can certainly delay the adoption of the budget. But they won’t, even though they have warned that negotiations will begin, rather than end, once EU member states agree on their figures. So there is a lot at stake.

Several leaders, including Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten, insisted there is no real deadline, but all of them know that pushing the talks deep into 2027 is risky.

Read more

Dutch dismiss any deadline on budget deal as EU leaders remain divided on size and new resources of revenue

Officially, it is true: there is no end-of-the-year deadline.

But Macron has warned that negotiations cannot drag on into 2027, when his country heads into an election in which far-right eurosceptic (and currently likely next president) Marine Le Pen has pledged to reopen any deal, reduce France’s contribution and stop Ukraine financing. 

A deal before deadline would protect the budget against later changes.

Red lines? They end up getting smudged

]]> Spain’s Hernández de Cos tapped to succeed fellow ‘owl’ Lagarde as ECB president https://euobserver.com/251927/spains-pablo-hernandez-de-cos-tapped-to-succeed-fellow-owl-lagarde-as-ecb-president/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:29:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251927 Neither dove nor hawk, the former Bank of Spain governor describes himself as an 'owl' when it comes to monetary policy, just like his predecessor Christine Lagarde did when she took over the helm in 2019. ]]> European leaders first tapped Spain’s former central bank chief Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) back in February. 

Other positions on the bank’s leadership board will also be filled, with the choice falling on German economist Markus Brunnermeier for the chief economist post and former OECD chief economist Laurence Boone as head of market operations on behalf of France.

The agreement was reached on the sidelines of a summit in Brussels on Thursday (26 November), but formal approval is expected at the next EU leaders’ summit in December.

De Cos, who governed the Bank of Spain between 2018 and 2024 and now heads the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements, will be the first Spaniard to lead the ECB. 

He beat the Dutch former central bank chief Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, after Paris and Berlin struck a deal in recent weeks that also divided up the other two leadership positions.

Lagarde announced in October that she will step down early, on 7 February, ahead of next year’s presidential election in France.

Read more

What kind of ECB is Europe getting after Lagarde?

“The Spanish government welcomes the European Council’s unanimous support for Pablo Hernández de Cos’s candidacy,” said a Spanish ministry representative, who also said that the election of a Spaniard to lead the bank was “excellent news for Spain and, above all, for Europe”.

After leaders discussed the candidates for the three positions on Thursday, ambassadors still had to meet and agree on one candidate for each post.

]]> Mass-produced, small, and cheap Russian missiles could shape the war in 2027, making Ukrainian cities into constant targets (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,736) https://euobserver.com/251867/mass-produced-small-and-cheap-russian-missiles-could-shape-the-war-in-2027-making-ukrainian-cities-into-constant-targets-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1736/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:41:52 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251867 A massive ramp-up in low-cost Russian missiles risks turning Ukrainian cities, power plants, and factories into constant targets, just as Kyiv struggles to finance interceptors and its own long‑range weapons. ]]>
  • Russia plans to produce 30,000 Banderol small cruise missiles next year. Why is this a problem?
  • They are faster than jet-powered drones, but cheaper than conventional Kh-101 missiles.
  • The Russian Rybar channel wrote that Ukrainians are conducting an offensive near Borove.
  • Chart of the day: A comparison of Ukraine’s Flamingo and Neptune missiles favours the latter, although both have their advantages.
  • Photo of the day: A detailed image of the Crimean Bridge.
  • Videos of the day: Ukrainians shot down a jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time; a Russian mechanised attack towards Dobropillia.

    • There has been much discussion in recent months about Russian jet-powered drones. Russia deployed 4,000 of them in October.

    The same applies to ballistic missiles, which Ukrainians lack Patriot interceptors to shoot down. According to Ukrainian defence minister Yevhen Khmara, Russian industry will produce nearly 150 of them per month.

    Another Russian weapon that receives less attention could also prove important to the course of the war in 2027. These are small Russian cruise missiles manufactured under the names Banderol, Dan-T, and Filin.

    We wrote about them in the summer, when they began, among other things, to destroy ships near the Ukrainian city of Odesa.

    Their significance has grown since then. While Russia was able to produce 80 of these missiles in August, according to the Defence Express website, by October 360 had been produced and fired at Ukrainian cities and positions.

    Production of these fast and relatively inexpensive missiles is set to expand significantly next year. They could become an even greater problem for Ukrainians than jet-powered drones.

    ]]>         Magyar shows what Hungary’s new policy on Ukraine could look like (Day 198 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/251827/magyar-shows-what-hungarys-new-policy-on-ukraine-could-look-like-day-198-of-the-tisza-government/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:08:14 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251827 Péter Magyar plays volleyball with Volodymyr Zelensky, but vows no blank cheque for Kyiv. He is simultaneously hitting Hungary’s oligarchs with a new wealth tax, sidelining Orbán loyalists from sports and culture, and watching Fidesz-friendly pollsters admit his party is now well ahead. ]]> The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

    • Parliament passes a wealth tax and reinstates the KATA tax scheme.
    • What did Péter Magyar’s visit to Ukraine achieve?
    • Politicians are being ousted from football club leadership.
    • The government is dismantling Orbán’s legacy in culture and education.
    • Poll of the week: Even a Fidesz-aligned pollster now puts the party behind.

    No Hungarian prime minister had visited Ukraine since 2015, Péter Magyar wrote ahead of his visit to Transcarpathia on Tuesday (24 November). He later clarified that he meant Transcarpathia. Viktor Orbán made a surprise trip to Kyiv in the summer of 2024, when Hungary held the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union. That trip was very different from Magyar’s visit this week.  

    In July 2024, Orbán held a brief press conference with Volodymyr Zelensky without taking questions, then quickly returned home. The visit was overshadowed by a call at the time from Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó to his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov. Three days later, Orbán travelled to Moscow for talks with Vladimir Putin. Orbán’s “peace mission” set off a diplomatic storm in the EU.  

    Magyar’s new policy on Ukraine

    Magyar’s trip took a very different form. For security reasons, his exact destination and the location of his meeting with the Ukrainian president could not be disclosed in advance, but he posted regular updates on social media.

    A day earlier, he had already made important gestures towards Ukraine in the Hungarian parliament, most notably by firmly distancing himself from Orbán’s aggressive and hostile policy towards the country.  

    Magyar and Zelensky first laid wreaths at soldiers’ graves in Uzhhorod, then visited a hospital and a Hungarian-language secondary school in Berehove. At the school they played volleyball. The footage made headlines around the world and showed more vividly than any statement that relations between Hungary and Ukraine had entered a new era.

    Magyar brought “absolute cinema” to Ukraine, too.

    Magyar managed to address several competing interests. He reached out to his Western allies and to Ukraine, framed his message around the concerns of Transcarpathia’s Hungarian community, and held to his firm position on funding for Ukraine and its accession to the EU.

    Fidesz’s fierce anti-Ukrainian campaign had left a deep mark on Hungarian voters and put Magyar in a difficult position. Tuesday’s visit gave his critics little to seize on. He struck a friendly tone with his Ukrainian counterparts while giving his critics little grounds to accuse him of bowing to Kyiv.

    Orbán did not comment on Magyar’s visit to Ukraine.

    Fidesz issued only a tepid statement calling on the prime minister to “make clear that Hungarians’ money will not go to Ukraine and that the war will not be funded with Hungarians’ money”.

    Magyar had effectively done just that while standing beside Zelensky in Berehove, leaving Fidesz little room for further criticism.

    New wealth tax

    The introduction of a wealth tax is one of the most contentious provisions in the Tisza government’s tax package. During the election campaign, Orbán repeatedly sought to alarm voters about Tisza’s proposed wealth tax. In his latest interview with the pro-Russian channel Ultrahang, Orbán reserved his fiercest criticism of the Tisza government for its economic policy, arguing that its tax increases would suffocate the Hungarian economy.  

    Read more

    MEPs still split over ending Hungary’s Article 7 sanctions procedure, but Magyar’s reforms win praise

    The wealth tax was passed with two rates. A one-percent rate will apply to wealth above HUF 1 billion (around €2.8m), and a 1.5 percent rate to wealth above HUF 100 billion. The higher rate will affect the wealthiest businesspeople, most of whom made their fortunes as oligarchs under Orbán.

    The tax will be paid by Hungarian-resident individuals and by taxpayers engaged in asset management. It will also apply to assets held abroad and to assets held in Hungary by foreign owners.

    The Tisza government expects the new tax to raise HUF 200 billion (around €550m) as early as 2027.

    As Telex reports, critics argue that the new tax could drive capital out of Hungary, divert funds from investment, impose a heavy administrative burden and affect many owners of smaller businesses.  

    It remains unclear whether president András Baka will sign the bill into law.

    KATA scheme revamped

    Another major tax change is parliament’s approval of the return of KATA, a simplified tax scheme for small businesses.

    In the summer of 2022, the Fidesz government changed the rules so that most self-employed people could no longer use it. The move provoked widespread anger just months after Orbán and his party won their biggest election victory.

    The Tisza government has now made it possible for self-employed people who invoice companies to use KATA. People who run a business alongside their main job will also be eligible again.

The European Court of Auditors interrogated the disbursement of funds in Germany, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Portugal and Poland.]]> Controls implemented by the EU failed to ensure money from so-called ‘green bonds’ was invested in environmentally-beneficial projects, with some of the funds spent on oil- and gas-fuelled assets.

    That’s according to a report published on Wednesday (25 November) by the European Court of Auditors, showing that the bloc’s environmental expenditure was sometimes not green, and that at other times the money could not be traced.

    Green bonds were issued by the EU Commission to help finance NextGenerationEU (NGEU), a recovery and resilience fund for post-Covid economic growth. 

    Out of 60 projects reviewed by auditors, eight materially overstated green spending, with auditors estimating that across seven member states, an estimated €5.5bn (9.8 percent) of €56.8bn may have been overstated.

    Issuing the bonds made the EU a major issuer of green debt, and bloc rules require member states to use at least 37 percent of their recovery money on sustainability. “We have identified ways to strengthen the existing framework [… ] This could also be important if the EU decides to issue green bonds again,” said lead auditor Jorg Kristijan Petrovič.

    In 2023, the European Green Bond Standard (EuGBS) was adopted by the EU as part of new green regulations. But since NGEU bonds began to be issued in 2021, this money was never the subject of new sustainable financing rules.

    The fact that bond spending did not meet the commission’s own standards “may create a perception of inconsistency,” according to the audit.

    “[The commission’s] own NGEU green bonds are not fully aligned with the EuGBS’s more stringent requirements,” the audit found. It also said there is no target for NGEU green bonds to align fully with the EU taxonomy in the future.

    Read more

    Auditors warn of ‘self-monitoring’ problem in EU aid cash spent by UN, amid growing funding row

    Non-green projects funded

    The report interrogated the disbursement of funds in seven countries – Germany, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Portugal and Poland – who together accounted for 88 percent of eligible green expenditure.

    ]]>         Lula’s online ‘army’ shows how copying Brazil’s WhatsApp model could backfire on Spain’s and France’s left https://euobserver.com/251777/lulas-online-army-shows-how-copying-brazils-whatsapp-model-could-backfire-on-spains-and-frances-left/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:00:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251777 With Spain voting on Sunday and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian 'digital army' experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right's dominance of online political communication. But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula's victory, his online army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.]]> Europe’s Left believes it may have found a formula for defeating the far-right.

    Following Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election last month, progressive movements in France and Spain began replicating the digital mobilisation strategy developed by congressman André Janones, whose WhatsApp channel, Exército do Lula (Lula’s Army), attracted nearly 11 million followers.

    With Spain voting on Sunday (29 November) and France preparing for its 2027 presidential election, the Brazilian experiment appears to offer an appealing solution to the far-right’s dominance of online political communication. 

    But there is a problem: barely a month after Lula’s victory, his digital army has found a new enemy and it’s not the far-right, but the Left itself.

    The channel that once mobilised millions against Bolsonaro is now being used to attack leftwing politicians and activists who oppose the government’s proposed fiscal adjustment – that was swiftly approved with the full support of the far-right.

    Read more

    Trump cheers Bolsonaro Jr’s advance on Lula in Brazil, but EU fears for Mercosur alliance

    Among its targets are members of the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), that supported the re-election of Lula da Silva, critics concerned about the potential consequences of fiscal restraint for public services and the poor, and even politicians of the president’s own Workers’ Party (PT).

    Janones has accused sections of the left of sabotaging Lula’s government, while more than 1.4 million followers have reportedly abandoned his channel since the election.

    The irony is difficult to ignore as a digital instrument celebrated for defending democracy against authoritarianism and the dangers of a new far-right government is now being deployed to discourage legitimate democratic disagreement.

    Lessons for Europe

    And this is precisely what European progressives should be examining before rushing to import Janones’ methods.

    There is no denying the effectiveness of his electoral strategy since through carefully coordinated messaging, viral content and instructions to millions of followers, Janones helped challenge Flavio Bolsonaro’s formidable digital machinery.

    Yet the electoral success of this operation should not obscure its fundamental limitations: mobilising millions of people to distribute political messages is not the same as empowering them to participate in political decisions.

    What happens when the candidate wins? Are those supporters expected to continue following orders, defending every government decision, regardless of their political convictions?

    That appears to be the contradiction confronting Lula’s Army.

    Its followers were instrumentalised as political combatants, receiving instructions about what to share, amplify and attack but they were never part of a democratic organisation capable of collectively deciding its political direction.

    When supporters began expressing dissatisfaction with Lula’s fiscal proposals, many responded to messages with scissors emojis, symbolising their opposition to potential spending cuts. Rather than engaging with their objections, Janones turned against critics within the left.

    It is an especially troubling development considering the historical relationship between Lula’s Workers’ Party and competing leftwing movements.

    In 2003, the PT expelled parliamentarians who opposed Lula’s pension reform, helping precipitate the creation of PSOL. During Brazil’s mass demonstrations in June 2013, the party struggled to understand the mobilisation and mostly backed the repression that followed.

    The Brazilian experience also raises uncomfortable questions about the growing dependence of progressive politics on personalised leadership and privately controlled digital platforms as WhatsApp channels can disseminate information with extraordinary efficiency, but they cannot, by themselves, replace trade unions, grassroots organisations, political assemblies or the slower, often frustrating process of democratic deliberation.

    A movement of millions that cannot meaningfully question its leadership may be an impressive electoral machine, but it is hardly a democratic revolution, and this is where the lessons for Europe become particularly urgent.

    MFF is the acronym for the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework. The next one will run from 2028 to 2034. If you’ve ever followed the tough negotiations in EU countries over their annual budgets, you can only imagine how difficult it is for 27 countries to agree on a seven-year budget.

    So, today’s and tomorrow’s gathering of EU leaders is just one of many meetings aimed at reaching an agreement on the MFF. This time, the goal is to narrow the gap between the 27 countries and hopefully pave the way for a deal in December.

    Because the question isn’t simply how much money Europe should spend. It’s also about what the EU should prioritise, and how it should pay for it.

    Reactions have been mixed. Many governments, particularly in southern and eastern Europe, want to protect existing spending, especially on agriculture and regional development.

    Others want the EU to invest more in industrial development, innovation and competitiveness. And there are also countries that are simply reluctant to see the overall budget increase, or to contribute more money.

    Costa’s proposal tries to strike a balance between these competing demands. He therefore proposes to reduce the overall size of the budget compared with the Commission’s initial proposal, while introducing new sources of revenue for the EU, so that member states don’t have to shoulder the entire financial burden themselves.

    The problem is always: where do you cut? In the latest proposal, the biggest reductions would affect the competitiveness part of the budget. That’s a sensitive issue because European leaders have spent the past few years insisting that Europe needs to invest more in its economy, support businesses and innovation, and compete with the US and China.

    But at the same time, there are very few areas where governments are willing to cut spending. Agriculture and regional development, for instance, remain particularly sensitive.     The parliament is also pushing for a more ambitious budget, arguing that the EU needs more resources to deal with the challenges ahead.

    And that brings us to another part of Costa’s proposal: how to generate more money for the EU.

    One of the options he has put forward is a digital tax. The idea is to introduce a three percent tax on certain large companies operating in Europe. It would apply to companies with an annual global turnover of more than €750m and more than €50m in turnover in the EU from digital activities.

    Read more

    With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter?

    We’re talking mainly about large tech companies. Smaller European firms, such as Mistral AI, would not fall under these thresholds, at least for now. This tax could generate around €5bln a year, or roughly €35bln over the seven-year budget period.

    The merit of president Costa’s negotiating box is to highlight that further proposals for new own resources are possible: it is time to fully explore them.

    We are campaigning to ensure that citizens’ voices are heard: the negotiations cannot be a matter for a handful of people behind closed doors, but should be open to the millions of people who are going to be the most affected by these decisions. The people we represent.

    We will gather on 9 December, from 1215 to 1330 in Place Schuman, to make citizens’ voices be heard, and we invite anyone who cares about the future of Europe to join us.

    We urge European leaders to go beyond closed-door negotiations, listen to the voices of the millions of people and communities affected, and deliver a result that is up to the challenges ahead. Anything less than that would be a failure whose price our grandchildren will still pay.

  • An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv.

The war there is concentrated primarily on the front line,” Robert Fico said on Wednesday (25 November) morning at the Slovak parliament’s European affairs committee, following his recent visit to Lviv, in Western Ukraine.

    He also reiterated to MPs that Slovakia would not support the €45bn loan for Ukraine. He described the European Commission’s effort to split it into two parts, with €25bn going to military aid and €20bn to civilian aid, as “a trick by the Commission”.

    Fico made these remarks just two days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called on him to show solidarity with Poland, whose territory was hit by Russian cruise missiles. “I do not know whether this appeal will touch your soul, but I am certain that this issue will determine Europe’s future,” Tusk said about aid to Ukraine.

    ]]>         A Russian plan to federalise Moldova could give it a window to control access to EU membership https://euobserver.com/251069/a-russian-plan-to-federalise-moldova-could-give-it-a-window-to-control-access-to-eu-membership/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:45:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251069 A reported Russian plan to federalise Moldova would hand the Kremlin a lever over who joins the EU. Europe should rule it out before it reaches the table.]]> Moscow’s strategy in its negotiations with Ukraine is no secret. The war’s resolution is no longer the sole subject of bilateral talks, but rather one item in a long list of maximalist demands. Russia now demands a new “security architecture” for all of Europe, with the war’s end a secondary priority. 

    It is not hard to compare this stance with Russia’s December 2021 ultimatum, demanding that Nato members commit to no further enlargement of the alliance and a ban on Nato activity in Eastern Europe. Moldova, yet again, finds itself directly at the centre of Russia’s confrontation with the West. 

    In late November 2003, Vladimir Putin was preparing to fly to Chișinău to witness the signing of the Kozak Memorandum, a Russian plan to turn Moldova into an asymmetric federation in which the breakaway region of Transnistria would hold a blocking vote over national decisions. The plan collapsed the night before.

    Under heavy Western pressure, Moldova’s leadership withdrew its consent, and Putin never boarded the plane.

    Twenty-three years later, the same idea appears to be back. This time, the idea is subsumed within the negotiations over Ukraine. Europe risks watching from the corridor.

    Read more

    War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement

    Russian outlet Eho, citing sources close to the talks, reported this week that Moscow is seeking to restructure Moldova as a federation of Moldova, Transnistria and Gagauzia, with independence referendums in the two regions should Moldova join the European Union.

    The proposal would reportedly also include the withdrawal of Russian troops from Transnistria in exchange for a Moldovan commitment not to join any military alliance. The report is unconfirmed. But its logic fits Russian policy so closely that European capitals cannot afford to dismiss it.

    Read more

    [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

    A veto over enlargement

    The most dangerous element is the referendum clause, because it targets the EU itself. Moldova’s 1994 law on Gagauzia already grants the region a right to external self-determination, if Moldova’s status as an independent state changes.

    The reported proposal would attach an explicit secession trigger to EU membership.

    If incorporated into a settlement, this provision would attach the threat of territorial fragmentation to Moldova’s European integration. The referendum need never take place for that threat to shape accession.

    Any Moldovan government would have to pursue membership knowing that it could trigger a new secession crisis. Moscow would gain a means of obstructing accession through Moldova’s internal politics.

    Russia’s economic leverage in Transnistria has weakened, with Gazprom’s direct supplies stopping in January 2025, while the EU accounted for 76.9 per cent of the region’s exports in the first half of 2026.

    A settlement of the kind reported would offer Moscow a means of converting that weakening material leverage into a lasting role in Moldova’s constitutional order. 

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

    Moscow has responded with escalating threats. Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that Moscow would treat any attempt to force reunification as an act of war against Russia.

    More recently, Russia’s envoy to the OSCE claimed that Chișinău’s fiscal policy toward the region could provoke a new military confrontation. Moscow is treating the extension of Moldova’s fiscal rules as grounds for escalation.

    Gagauzia has no frozen conflict, no separatist army and no line of contact, despite latent tensions. Its inclusion extends the proposal beyond settling the Transnistrian conflict and into restructuring Moldova’s national decision-making.

    A federal settlement granting Moscow-aligned regional leaderships blocking powers over national decisions could extend Russian influence into Moldova’s central institutions.

    Read more

    EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

    What Europe should do

    This is where Europe’s responsibility begins. Washington is in a hurry to close a deal, and a small candidate country on Europe’s periphery can look like a cheap concession from across the Atlantic. It is not cheap for the EU.

    The EU has opened accession negotiations with Moldova, committed €1.9bn through its Growth Plan and is now funding its air defences.

    All of that would be hollowed out by a settlement that hands Moscow a lever over Moldova’s constitution.

    Europe does not need a new policy, only to use the leverage it already has. First, the EU and its member states should state publicly that Moldova’s constitutional order and its accession path are not negotiable in any format without Moldova.

    Second, the mandate of Europe’s negotiator should include the full withdrawal of Russian troops and munitions as an unfulfilled Russian obligation. In May, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas argued that Russian withdrawal from Transnistria should be one of the EU’s demands in negotiations with Moscow. That demand should be explicit in any European negotiating mandate. That promise should now be written down.

    Third, Europe should refuse any sanctions relief or return of Russian gas while Russian troops remain on the territory of an EU candidate. 

    Chișinău should turn its existing reintegration measures into a clearer political offer, with explicit guarantees for residents of the left bank, and Brussels should be ready to support it.

    It should put forward its own reintegration offer, with clear guarantees for residents of Transnistria within a unitary state, and Brussels should be ready to fund it. If there is no plan from Chișinău and Brussels on the table, it will consider one from Moscow.

      <title>China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/26/brazil-china-react-to-new-trump-tariffs-threat</link>
      <description><p>Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe">Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU</a></p></li></ul><p>Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.</p><p>Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/26/brazil-china-react-to-new-trump-tariffs-threat">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/trump-tariffs">Trump tariffs</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/china">China</category>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/brazil">Brazil</category>

      <title>Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses</link>
      <description><p>Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August</p><p>The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/18/abc-sues-trump-federal-communications-commission">sued the agency</a> in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.</p><p>The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age</link>
      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>
