<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 27 Nov 2026 01:50:41 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Roofing company fined €60,000 over death of worker after fall at Cork school]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/11/26/roofing-company-fined-60000-over-death-of-worker-after-fall-at-cork-school/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/11/26/roofing-company-fined-60000-over-death-of-worker-after-fall-at-cork-school/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 19:58:00 +0000A Co Cork-based roofing company has been fined €60,000 in relation to the death seven years ago of Brian McGrath who suffered a fatal fall while working on the roof of a school near Mitchelstown.

McGrath, who left a wife and three young children, was 39 at the time of the incident at Kildorrery National School in 2019.

His widow Anne told Cork Circuit Criminal Court on Thursday that the lives of the family had been changed forever and that she and her children were still trying to cope with the devastation. “We will carry the consequences of that moment for the rest of our lives,” she said.

McGrath’s employer, NCA Roofing, pleaded guilty to three breaches of the Health and Safety at Work Act 2005 at the court sitting, where Judge Helen Boyle imposed the fine.

Health and Safety Authority (HSA) inspector Trevor Ryan Nesbitt told the court that an investigation found McGrath had fallen from a height of approximately 3m into a classroom and hit his head. It appeared he had stood on timber strut between the joists that gave way beneath him.

It was discovered that a proper method of working with asbestos was not in place, whereby power tools were used to cut tiles containing the material, creating airborne dust.

Company principal Patrick Butler pleaded guilty to three offences including failing to ensure a safe place of work for working at a height, namely there was the absence of a protective rail to safeguard against a fall and the absence of scaffold, airbags or beanbags underneath in the event of a fall.

The second, related charge, to which Butler pleaded guilty, concerned the failure to organise and plan a safe method of working at a height while the third count, to which he pleaded guilty, was of failing to provide appropriate training for staff exposed to asbestos.

Defence counsel Donal O’Sullivan said his client had been in business since 1993 and had not come to the adverse attention of the HSA before or since this incident. Part of their business is roofing work at rural schools, he said.

“Patrick Butler would not be the kind of person who would be sending people to do jobs that he would not do himself. He would be getting up on the roof as much as anybody to do the work himself,” said O’Sullivan, adding that his client was deeply remorseful.

He said that the company was fully insured and the fatal incident did not arise out of some attempt by the company to maximise profits or to put someone at risk.

McGrath was reported to be very popular in the local community and a GoFundMe page for his family raised more than €13,000 after his death.

Responding to the conviction, HSA assistant chief executive Eibhlin O’Leary said: “Falls from height remain one of the most serious risks in the construction sector.

“Employers and those in control of work activities must ensure that appropriate measures are in place to prevent falls, including where there are openings or fragile areas on a roof. These risks must be identified before work begins and appropriate controls put in place.”

Research published by the HSA last month found that of 23 construction sector fatalities from 2002 to 2024, 83 per cent occurred on a site with between one and four workers.

Almost all, 87 per cent, of those killed were aged over 35, and almost half, 10, were self-employed. Fifteen deaths were reported to be the result of falls.

Construction consistently accounts for the second highest number of workplace fatalities in Ireland, with agriculture repeatedly top of the annual list.

There were 177 fatalities on Irish farms between 2016 and last year, with 21 the result of results of falls from a height.

Older farmers working alone is also regarded as a key contributor to fatalities, a significant portion of which tend to involve farm machinery.

The fine imposed on NCA Roofing is the fourth imposed on an employer this month after a prosecution related to the death of an employee.

Brothers Seamus and Patrick McEvoy were fined €50,000 each following the death of a worker who fell from the roof of an agricultural building that was under construction in Ballacolla, Co Laois. Kavanagh Retailing, trading as Kavanagh SuperValu in Westport, was fined €125,000 after a member of the public was struck and killed by a delivery vehicle.

Cyprus-based Matrix Ship Management, which provides crew and management services to Irish Ferries, was fined €200,000 in relation to the death of Sergejs Lescenko in March 2019. He was crushed between two trailers while working on the loading of a car deck.

]]><![CDATA[Here’s why Irish pension holders should pay attention to the tech sell-off and what is to come]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/26/the-nvidia-saga-and-the-ai-bubble-really-matter-for-your-pension-fund/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/26/the-nvidia-saga-and-the-ai-bubble-really-matter-for-your-pension-fund/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:04:11 +0000Do Irish pension holders need to be worried about the tech sell-off which has hit markets in recent weeks? The Nasdaq index of US shares – largely driven by tech – has lost some 10 per cent and is now up just 1.4 per cent for the year.

The wider S&P500 has lost 8 per cent since its October peak, though is still up nearly 5 per cent since January. Seasoned investors who subscribed for the recent Anthropic flotation and may have holdings on stocks such as Nvidia will, indeed, be biting their nails.

Anthropic shares soared after the recent flotation but at Wednesday’s close were slightly below their $83 (€75.60) float price.

As for Nvidia, who knows what will happen next, though the share surge following the reappointment of Jensen Huang quickly ran out of steam.

But what about ordinary Irish pension fund holders, or perhaps those who have invested cash into exchange-traded funds or other instruments linked to equity markets?

The US has such a big share of world markets that any fund with a share of global equities will be invested here – and this means holding stakes in the big artificial intelligence (AI) players too, given their outsized share of the market. Your pension will in all likelihood have holdings in Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple and, before long, Anthropic.

So do investors need to worry about what has happened in recent weeks and what is to come?

A stake in AI

Your pension fund will typically be invested in a range of assets – principally equities, bonds and cash – and in most funds equities will take the largest share. The weightings will typically change over time, with less reliance on equities approaching retirement as a way to lower risk.

So for most pension holders, the big AI players will indeed form part of their portfolio. The fortunes of Jensen Huang and the success of Anthropic’s Claude AI models affect your pension. They have become so dominant in terms of the overall value of markets that this has become inevitable – and the huge gains have given funds a boost over the last few years.

Pension funds vary but Aidan Donnelly, head of global equities at Davy, points out that a pension fund would typically have 55 to 60 per cent invested in equities on average.

The US would typically account for 65 per cent of this index and, to take one example, Nvidia has a market weight of about 6 per cent so it might represent 2-2½ per cent-plus of a typical pension fund.

Figures produced by the pension industry for individual funds confirm this and in some cases the holdings are higher. In the Irish Life Forum 4 fund, for example, a typical mid- to higher-risk product which would be used to build up investment with retirement still a way off, the top 10 equities – all major US companies except for Taiwan Semiconductor – account for 24 per cent of the total fund value.

Five big US firms – Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon, account for 18 per cent, with Apple and Nvidia both at about 4.5 per cent. This has paid off this year, with the fund up close to 10 per cent to date despite the recent fall-off in US equities. And the rise in these shares has been stellar over the past few years with Nvidia rising from $50 three years ago to almost $150 now.

But the concentration risk of pension funds to these big players is there, nonetheless. And obviously the risk for those invested outside their pension in US-linked investment funds which match the big indices is all the greater.

The dollar bounce

The US dollar has risen against the euro this year – by close to 7 per cent. This has given a big bounce to Irish pension funds invested in the US when dollar investments are translated back to euro. Donnelly of Davys points out that despite the latest fall-off in US shares from their highs, the annual returns are still generally in double figures in euro terms. In turn this has been a big support to Irish pension funds this year.

The S&P 500 is up by close to 5 per cent from January but add in the impact of the rising US dollar and this brings the total gain in euro terms to about 12 per cent. This gain was 16 per cent in September, but the annual return is still very healthy for investors on this side of the Atlantic. Many Irish pension funds from the main providers are up 10-15 per cent year to date and even more cautious ones are up 7 to 10 per cent.

The AI risk

With funds heavily invested in the AI bubble and the wider US economy which depends on it, it is self-evident that there is a risk if the bubble “bursts”, or even if the more gentle generally downward trend in share prices seen in recent weeks were to continue.

Big international investment houses now publishing their outlooks for 2027 remain broadly upbeat, though conscious of the risks. UBS Securities, for example, says it believes investors should “stay in the market”, though concentrate on diversifying their portfolios in an environment of “elevated uncertainty”.

This uncertainty involves the much-discussed issue of whether the returns from AI will justify investor enthusiasm. With AI investment in the US set to rise, on UBS estimates from $1 trillion in 2026 – the bulk of which comes from the big players – to $1.6 trillion next year, the question is what return this will show and how quickly this will become evident.

If investment continues to outpace returns, investor fears will grow, as we have seen in recent weeks.

This poses a risk for pensions going into 2027. So too does the environment of rising interest rates, which could – if it worsens – lead to falls in the value of bond holdings, another mainstay of pensions. In 2022, both equities and bonds fell together, the nightmare scenario for funds.

Irish households now own nearly a €1 trillion worth of property assets, according to the Central Bank.

The regulator’s latest wealth report indicated that housing accounted for 67 per cent – or €956 billion – of the €1.43 trillion in wealth held by households here in the second quarter.

The total net wealth figure represents “a new series high,” the bank said.

It equates to about €245,000 per person, or €724,000 per household.

The wealth of households has risen in tandem with house prices which have doubled in a decade.

The latest quarterly was, however, driven by a rise in financial assets of €35.3 billion, with “positive revaluations” accounting for most of the increase.

Housing wealth increased by €11 billion over the quarter, also due to positive revaluations.

The net wealth of households is calculated by adding the total value of the housing stock and financial assets – such as cash savings, shares, pensions and possessions such as cars and antiques – and subtracting debt owed or liabilities.

It is considered a crude measure of prosperity as it hides the distribution of household assets and liabilities across income groups and age categories.

The latest figures highlight a very uneven distribution of wealth in Ireland, with the total net wealth of households in the poorest half of the distribution accounting for less than 10 per cent (€145 billion) of the national total.

By contrast, the top 10 per cent of Irish households owned €686.7 billion, 47 per cent, of total household net wealth in the State.

“As a result, the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households continued to hold nearly five times the amount held by households in the bottom half of the net wealth distribution all together,” the bank said.

Households in the middle part of the income distribution (deciles six to nine) owned €629.4 billion overall, or 43.1 per cent of total net wealth.

The balance-sheet composition of Irish households also differed significantly depending on the income level.

Households in the top 10 per cent net wealth decile displayed a more diversified portfolio composition with other financial assets (comprising debt securities, listed shares, investment fund shares and life insurance and annuity entitlements) featuring “prominently”, accounting for 19.4 per cent of total assets.

The bank also noted that wealthier households also displayed lower leverage (meaning they had less debt) when compared with households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution.

Conversely, households in the lower deciles held their financial wealth mainly in deposits (18.5 per cent of their total assets) and were significantly more leveraged (28.1 per cent).

Ella Gleeson, private client manager with wealth advisers NFP Ireland, said: “While today’s report shows that household wealth continues to rise in Ireland, increasing by almost €43 billion, rising living costs are putting pressure on disposable incomes and could make it harder for families to save, invest and build their wealth.

“Today’s report shows that a significant proportion of Irish household wealth is tied up in property,” she added. “While rising property values can make families wealthier on paper, that does not necessarily mean they have greater financial resilience.”

]]>Nathan Laine<![CDATA[Can my brother move into our elderly father’s house before our inheritance is finalised?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Q: A reader and his two siblings are to inherit their father’s home and savings in equal shares; he has told them so. But with their father, who is experiencing dementia, now in a nursing home, the siblings are worried about the house being empty. Could they rent it out?

The siblings are in agreement with a brother’s plan to move into the house when he retires and their father has died. He would buy out the other two. But could the brother move in now, settling up with his siblings later from the proceeds of the will?

“If this person was in my consultation room, the very first priority is to go home and find the insurance policy,” says Andrea Clarke, principal solicitor at Coyne Solicitors.

“If the property isn’t insured and it burns down, there is no asset,” says Clarke.

The insurer will need to be informed that the house is unoccupied.

The reader’s father was an organised man. As well as sharing his will with his children, he registered an enduring power of attorney (EPA). The reader is the trusted person he appointed to make decisions on his behalf.

This EPA is now being enacted, the reader says. But the EPA alone may not give his son the power to rent out the property or allow his brother to move in.

My mother got an inheritance and a gift from her parents – can she reduce her tax bill?

“Your obligation first and foremost is to carry out the father’s wishes in his will and under the EPA,” says Clarke.

The primary concern should be their father’s care now.

“There is no entitlement for the children to have the house until the father passes away.

“You can’t make decisions in relation to the house or give it to a brother unless the EPA explicitly permits that,” says Clarke.

The reader may need to get court approval to move forward, says Clarke.

If the court did allow the property to be transferred to the brother, capital acquisitions tax (CAT) and capital gains tax would all have to be dealt with now, she says.

Revenue won’t wait until the father dies to be paid the tax.

If the father is availing of the Fair Deal scheme, where his income and assets contribute to paying for his nursing home, the HSE will have a say too, says Clarke.

The HSE might be quite happy for it to be rented, maximising their return. New rules, however, mean tenancies now run in rolling six-year cycles. A tenancy can only be ended mid-cycle on very limited grounds.

“The death of their father would not be a reason to terminate a lease mid-cycle,” says Clarke. This means the siblings may not get vacant possession of the house when they want it.

Renting it on Airbnb, if the EPA and local planning rules allow it, would be more flexible, but it would entail work.

I’m giving my son a €490,000 property. Can I cut tax bill by giving part of it as a loan?

Another option is to rent the house to the brother, but it would have to be at market rent, says Clarke.

Alternatively, the brother could move into the house under a “caretaker’s agreement”, effectively providing a service to the family by occupying the property, says Clarke.

This would have to be carefully drafted so as not be interpreted as a tenancy that could cause problems if the siblings were to fall out.

The caretaker’s agreement would need to address any EPA or court requirements. The HSE, however, may not want someone living in the property for free when renting it would generate income.

If the brother does move under a caretaker’s agreement, he could then seek dwelling house relief – this would allow him to inherit the house tax-free, without using up his tax-free CAT threshold, says Clarke.

He would need to live in the house as his main residence for the three years immediately before his father’s death and have no beneficial interest in another property, and he must live in the house for six years after he has inherited it, to claim the relief.

Can we continue renting to our Ukrainian friends and reclaim our holiday home later?

“The father could die sooner, he might not get that three-year period,” says Clarke.

If the family does go this route, then when their father dies, they could complete a “deed of family arrangement”, she says.

This isn’t about the siblings changing the will, but changing how the assets are distributed.

“The will says everything gets divided between the three of them, but all the beneficiaries could agree that one brother gets the house and the other two get the money,” says Clarke.

A deed of family arrangement must be completed within two years of their father’s death and before the grant of probate is extracted.

If there isn’t enough money in the estate for everyone to get an equal share, they could agree to an equalisation payment to square things up.

As his father’s personal representative, the reader could alternatively distribute the assets “in specie”, under the rules of appropriation.

Just like the deed of family arrangement, this is not a free hand to rewrite the will, but he could give the house to the brother with the bank savings going to himself and his sister, so long as this is consistent with the beneficiaries rights under the will, says Clarke.

An equalisation payment may need to be made here too.

“Making a really well written caretaker’s agreement allowing the brother to go into the property now and taking the subsequent steps could potentially be the most tax-efficient thing for them to do,” says Clarke.

So, the brother would sell his own house and move into the father’s house. Qualifying for dwelling house relief will depend on his father living for three years.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[US comedy gag about a sister who quits job to care for dad is no joke]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000

If you didn’t laugh, you may have cried – or maybe you did both – after watching Saturday Night Live’s Sister sketch when it flooded into family and friends’ messaging apps earlier this month.

In the American comedy programme’s skit, a son realises his ageing father needs more care at home but he doesn’t want to put Dad in a nursing home and live-in care could cost thousands.

He says: “I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live-in 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free and also … your sister.

“Signing up couldn’t be easier. Simply text ‘Dad fell’ to Sister and she will quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him.”

She manages medications, handles doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, and can even bring her reluctant husband along – all without affecting the son’s 50 per cent share of the inheritance – because the parents’ will predates their dementia. Now, the son says, “I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

The parody ends with “Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has a good therapist.”

The comedy lands so well because it’s painfully true. “When care intensifies, women’s employment pays the price,” according to the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). When care is unavailable, unaffordable or does not meet families’ needs, someone has to fill the gap. Too often, that someone is a woman.

“What may begin as a private decision about how a family organises care can therefore have very broad consequences for employment, income and gender equality,” says EIGE.

Of course, plenty of men look after their parents and children, too. But as care responsibilities intensify over time, it’s women who are substantially more likely than men to leave employment. Lower-income carers, who tend to be women, are most exposed to care-related employment penalties. EIGE says “27 per cent of lower-income carers report reducing working hours or leaving employment due to care, compared with 20 per cent of middle-income carers and 17 per cent of higher-income carers”.

The big squeeze

With an estimated one in nine people in the workforce both caring for a loved one and managing their career, employers need to start future-proofing their employee benefits. The numbers are probably going only one way due to our ageing population but supports, both private and public, are limited.

In Ireland, employer-funded carer supports fall into two main categories: dedicated paid carer leave, which is still rare, and structured, carer-friendly workplace programmes. which are unpaid and more common in large employers.

The State offers limited supports for carers. Under the Carer’s Leave Act, eligible employees can take unpaid leave of between 13 and 104 weeks to provide full-time care to a qualifying person. Employees may qualify for Department of Social Protection payments such as carer’s benefit (PRSI-based) or carer’s allowance (means-tested). There’s also statutory medical care leave of up to five days of unpaid leave in a 12-month period.

Family Carers Ireland (FCI) estimates there are more than 624,000 family carers, and that at least 270,000 are balancing paid work with care. FCI thinks the number of working carers is even higher than that, as many people do not see themselves as carers. They see themselves simply as wives, daughter, sons or neighbours.

When South East Technological University surveyed its staff after joining FCI’s Caring Employers programme, 60 per cent identified as family carers. Most employers simply never ask this question, so the numbers are hard to quantify.

Ibec’s Better Care Better Business report, published in March 2024, gives us a snapshot of what this costs carers who also work outside the home. Of the carers surveyed, 63 per cent were in employment and 73 per cent of those found it challenging to balance work and care. Some 57 per cent reported added financial pressure and more than a third said caring had affected their careers.

Carers are often exhausted and don’t know where to turn for support. While 57 per cent said their employer had been flexible, only 29 per cent were aware of a company policy on caring and just 21 per cent had ever received paid leave for it. Most support seems to depend on company or managerial goodwill.

‘I care for my elderly parents, but my efforts are taken for granted. I think I might be going mad’

FCI’s State of Caring 2026 report, based on responses from 2,930 carers, describes the reality of informal unpaid supports. Some 71 per cent say caring has harmed their health, and the same proportion find it difficult to make ends meet.

When caring responsibilities become unmanageable, employees are often forced to make difficult choices. Some reduce their hours, others take extended leave and many leave the workforce altogether, often permanently. Carers who remain in work report less loneliness than those who have left, which is one reason the charity wants carers kept in employment wherever possible.

Amongst women: Why are there so few men in caring roles?

The cost to employers in recruitment, training and lost institutional knowledge is significant, and it is largely avoidable. Unaddressed caregiving interruptions carry real costs, including an estimated €615 million annually in Ireland from eldercare-related work disruptions alone, says FCI.

Small, practical actions can make a meaningful difference to employees such as offering flexible working options, showing understanding during challenging periods, encouraging open and respectful conversations, providing access to leave and wellbeing supports, communicating information on rights and entitlements through human resources and fostering empathetic leadership.

‘All the caring I put into my parents – the time, effort and money – is gone, wasted’

Employer toolkit

  1. Find out who your carers are. Run an anonymous survey. Most will not volunteer the information and many do not use the word carer.
  2. Write a carer policy and publicise it. If only three in 10 carers know a policy exists, it’s not doing its job.
  3. Train line managers. When flexibility is granted informally, it’s only as good as the next manager.
  4. Offer to pay for some carer days beyond the legal requirement, and ensure that dependents include parents, in-laws and other relatives. Family comes in many shapes and sizes.
  5. Make flexibility two-way. Offer workers compressed or reduced hours with an agreed route back to full hours when care needs change.
  6. Introduce a carer passport so arrangements do not have to be renegotiated after every restructure or new manager.
  7. Provide practical information. In the middle of a crisis, most people first need to understand home supports, the Fair Deal scheme and enduring power of attorney. The local HSE home support office or public health nurse is often the first port of call.
  8. Plan for the carers you will have. With an ageing population, employees who are not carers today will be tomorrow so explore those pathways now.

So, what’s the real cost of the Sister gag? The punchline is that Sister is free. She’s not. The cost shows up in her health, her hours, her reduced pension pot and her lost promotion prospects. Eventually it shows up for her employer too, in turnover and lost experience, when she decides the only way to manage is to leave.

Employers can’t make relatives share the load. But they can stop assuming that someone’s sister – who might also be their best employee – will absorb it.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

Jensen Huang has the affair – his wife gets the performance review. Some things never change

In advance of the Christmas party season, we asked experts what happens if things go wrong. Who is liable?

Can employees face consequences, including dismissal, for any wrongful actions at such an affair?

The simple answer is yes.

Employees appreciate the chance to let their hair down and connect with colleagues outside of their usual working environment, says Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland. However, the combination of a relaxed atmosphere and the consumption of alcohol, some if not all of which is often free, can lead to “embarrassing moments, accidents, aggressive behaviour or even sexual misconduct”, she says.

Christmas parties are an extension of the workplace, Grassick says, “even if they take place off-site”, which means workplace policies and codes of conduct still apply, and employees can face disciplinary action if they breach those policies during the event.

Noting that employees might have different interpretations of “appropriate Christmas party behaviour”, Grassick says employers should issue a reminder of company policies ahead of time, saying they have a duty to ensure policies are communicated.

“We’ve all heard the nightmare tales of Christmas parties gone wrong, and it’s important for employers to mitigate risks where they can.

“It’s not a question of dampening the spirit of the event, but setting expectations early will help to ensure that no one wakes up the next day facing a disciplinary meeting as well as a hangover,” she says.

Grassick stresses HR professionals are “not the fun police”.

“We love a party as much as anyone, and the right preparations can allow for a festive party that is safe and enjoyable for everyone,” she says.

Jennifer Cashman, partner and head of employment at law firm RDJ, says an event organised, funded or endorsed by an employer can be regarded as an extension of the workplace, “even outside office hours”.

As such, employers can face liability for wrongful acts by employees during such events.

“Employers may have a defence where they prove they took the reasonably practicable steps required by legislation. Having a policy alone is insufficient. Communication, training and implementation matter.

“Importantly, conduct outside of the office can still lead to disciplinary action,” she says, including dismissal in serious cases.

Incidents after an official work event, including in hotel rooms or on the journey home, can also raise liability issues, she says.

My employer won’t let me carry over three days of leave to use in January. Is that allowed?

Employees can also bring personal injury claims against employers in the event of injury at Christmas parties, such as through falls, she says.

“Compensation is not automatic. The circumstances would need to be examined, including what caused the fall, who controlled the premises, whether a foreseeable risk was addressed and whether the employer took reasonably practicable precautions,” she says.

“These should explain expected conduct, unacceptable behaviour, reporting procedures and possible disciplinary consequences,” she says.

Set finishing times, “sensible limits” on alcohol availability and non-alcoholic options are practical steps that can help events run smoothly, she says.

Asked if liability can extend to after-work drinks organised independently by employees, Cashman says employer liability is less likely where there is no employer knowledge, funding or involvement.

“However, this is not a blanket exemption, particularly for employment-related harassment,” she says.

]]>Ignatiev<![CDATA[Spend your way to a holiday: Can the right bank card really get you free flights?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/25/spend-your-way-to-a-holiday-can-the-right-bank-card-really-get-you-free-flights/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/25/spend-your-way-to-a-holiday-can-the-right-bank-card-really-get-you-free-flights/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Can you turn your everyday spending into holidays? Some credit cards and debit cards offer free flights and travel perks linked to your spending.

If you have some big-ticket purchases coming up in 2027 then putting them on the right card in a planned way could send you on your next holiday.

So which cards will get you flying sooner? How much could you really save on flights? And is chasing rewards like this even worth it?

Rewards

Card rewards are big business in the United States. Card issuers there can charge far higher card fees than those in the European Union, giving them a bigger margin to fund benefits. Many Americans hold multiple cards just to chase the perks.

Although the rewards were once synonymous with glamorous travel, hotel or dining benefits, an equal number of US cardholders are now using their rewards to pay for essentials such as groceries and fuel.

In Europe, using debit cards and bank transfers is more common for everyday spending. Large-scale card rewards programmes are less part of our culture. But there are some credit and debit cards here that trumpet their travel perks, including free and discounted fares, travel insurance, airport lounge access and priority boarding.

Revolut is big on travel perks. Bank of Ireland was too – until last week. It is withdrawing the Aer Card, a credit card it offers in association with Aer Lingus. Aer cardholders could claim two free Aer Lingus flights and earn “Avios”, a loyalty currency used by several major airlines, at an accelerated pace.

Spend your gift vouchers as soon as you get them – there’s no point in waiting

The move follows criticisms about the difficulty in redeeming the Aer Lingus flight freebie.

Getting a free airfare for simply tapping your card feels like a good deal. But choosing a card for its travel rewards alone will be a false economy if the card membership fees, transaction charges, interest and the hassle of claiming your benefits outweigh the perks.

Credit cards in particular are an expensive form of borrowing. They make most sense if you can pay what you owe in full and on time. Setting up a direct debit to clear the full balance will prevent costly interest charges.

So spend within the lines, watch for fees and check for ease of booking and that the travel rewards offered by your card provider may be actual rewards.

Aer card

The recently discontinued Aer credit card, offered by Bank of Ireland in partnership with Aer Lingus, was all about the travel perks. Examining what was good and bad about this card is instructive.

The sales pitch was that once you hit spending of €5,000 or more in a “reward year” – so in the 12-month period starting from the date the credit card account was opened, you got two free return tickets on an Aer Lingus ticketed and operated service from Dublin, Cork, Shannon or Belfast to Europe.

There were other sweeteners, too: cardholders would automatically get two Aer Lingus “fast track” passes to get you through Dublin and Shannon Airport security, though fast track wasn’t available Cork.

You’d get two free Aer Lingus Lounge passes and two priority boarding passes every year, too. You also got multi-trip travel insurance for a family of four, including winter sports cover.

Bank of Ireland valued these sweeteners at “over €400 a year”.

So if you were going to spend €5,000 in the year anyway, your finances were robust and you trusted yourself to pay down your credit card balance when it fell due without incurring punitive interest, then you might have thought: “Why not?”

Did these perks add up?

First, there was a fee for the credit card of €6.50 a month and there’s the annual government stamp duty on all credit cards of €30. So whatever perks you were going to get should be worth more than €108 a year you were spending simply to have the credit card.

The free multi-trip travel insurance was a nice touch, but if you had private health insurance, this cover may already be included in your premium, or could be added for a small fee, making this perk redundant.

The Aer Lingus lounge has free sandwiches, snacks, coffees and juices. With food in the main airport costing an arm and a leg, this was arguably a useful perk. But the two passes could make some tough choices on a family holiday as children aged over two needed their own pass.

What about the free flights?

Two free return Aer Lingus flights to Europe for two people could definitely take the sting out of the cost of a summer holiday, a midterm break trip, a city break with friends or a Six Nations rugby weekend.

Except you were unlikely to be able to cash in your two Aer card free flights then.

Availability was restricted during peak travel periods, including but not limited to bank holidays, school holidays and sporting events, Aer Lingus said. They are particularly restricted on weekends, during school summer holidays, over Christmas and Easter and Irish bank holiday weekends.

So it’s possible your free return flight to Europe wasn’t going to be one you had planned to take anyway, but rather an extra one you ended up taking at a random time simply because it was free.

The reward flight included a free 10kg carry-on bag, but you still had to pay taxes, fees and charges on the flights. Users say these typically come to about €70 for two return flights.

Aer Lingus says there were just two Aer credit card seats available to book on each eligible flight.

But you couldn’t actually book your free flights through aerlingus.com – you couldn’t directly book at all. Instead, you submit a “request” to a separate credit card portal, specifying all your passenger information and a few different preferred dates.

Once you completed the form, you got a “case number” and an Aer Lingus agent contacted you about your case. So it was not as easy as booking a free flight of your choice.

Reddit users have plenty to say about this. Some describe the free flight request process as a “nightmare” and an “endless loop”.

Some users report it taking three or more attempts, submitting different possible travel dates and several weeks to get flights approved.

You had 12 months from the date you reached €5,000 in eligible spending to request the two free return fares otherwise you lost them. You could find yourself on a flight to Warsaw in November in a bid to use the only available freebie before your perk expired.

Book early and you were more likely to get your preferred destination and travel dates, Aer Lingus said.

Existing Aer credit cardholders can continue to try to book their free return flight through the portal in the usual way until November 30th, 2027, Aer Lingus says. But while you can fly until October 31st, 2028, your two free lounge and fast track passes expire a year earlier.

The card’s withdrawal is likely to generate a clamour of attempted bookings. As the existing quota of just two reward seats per eligible European flight remains, claiming your free flight could become harder still.

What’s the point?

Revolut customers can earn RevPoints. These can be converted one to one for “Avios” and redeemed in full or part payment towards flights with partner airlines, including Aer Lingus, British Airways and KLM.

RevPoints can be earned on eligible credit and debit card purchases at a rate linked to your Revolut plan – of which there are five.

For example, those using Revolut’s “Standard” plan debit card, which is free, earn one RevPoint for every €10 spent.

Gillian Harvey, her husband Mick and children Chloe and Sophie are big world travellers, having visited 38 countries.

“We are always looking at ways to save money on trips and get a little bit extra back from the spending we would be doing anyway,” Harvey says.

She tries to collect Avios points on everyday spending, putting these towards flights.

Harvey does that by spending on her Aer card and Revolut card and by converting her Tesco Clubcard points to Avios.

She watches out for promotions that enable 20 per cent more Avios points when converting.

Avios points helped towards a family trip to Florida this year.

“We use our Aer Lingus credit card for everyday spending, pay it off straight away and build up Avios towards flights,” says Harvey, who runs the Instagram account @wherearewegoingtomorrowtravel.

“We always make sure to pay the credit card balance in full, so we’re not paying any interest.

“The two free flights with the Aer card are a lovely added perk, but I wouldn’t choose the card solely for those, given the restrictions on availability.”

She is a member of the Aer Lingus AerClub loyalty programme, which is free. It runs the AerClub eStore, an online shopping portal where members can earn Avios by shopping with participating brands. Avios can be earned using any accepted card.

“You can earn points through retailers like Arnotts, Brown Thomas, Lifestyle Sports – it’s worth checking before you buy anything,” Harvey says.

“One thing I’ve learned is you need to go through the AerClub website first and click on the retailer you want to shop with for the points to track.

“It’s great around Christmas – when picking up gifts for others we are also earning points towards our next trip.”

She also recommends making sure everyone in the family has their own AerClub account and adding their membership numbers when booking flights to maximise points.

When the Aer card is discontinued next year, cardholders’ Avios will remain linked to their AerClub account, Aer Lingus says.

Which plan?

Revolut customers earn RevPoints at a rate linked to their Revolut plan.

For example, those using Revolut’s Standard plan debit card, which is free, earn one RevPoint for every €10 spent.

The Revolut Premium plan, which costs €9.99 a month, offers one RevPoint for every €4 on regular spending using a Revolut Premium debit card. This is the same Avios points-earning ratio as the Aer Lingus credit card.

Use the Revolut Premium credit card for the purchase instead and you get half a point more.

The annual percentage rate for Revolut credit cards is 17.99 per cent.

Revolut Metal and Revolut Ultra plans are a faster way to accumulate points towards airfares – but membership paid monthly costs €17.99 a month and €55 respectively, though €55 is an introductory offer.

With a Revolut Metal credit card, you will earn one RevPoint for every €1 spent. With an Ultra credit card, you will earn one and half RevPoints per €1 spent.

Premium, Metal and Ultra plans include travel insurance, with Ultra having broader car hire excess and cancellation cover.

With Ultra, you get unlimited complimentary airport lounge access at 1,600 airport lounges worldwide and unlimited fast track through security where it’s possible.

There are no currency exchange fees with these three Revolut plans. The Aer card for example charges 2.25 per cent of the transaction value for purchases in non-euro currencies.

Some of the higher-end Revolut plans bundle in lots of other things into membership, but here we are looking at travel perks.

Spend €5,000 on a Revolut Metal credit card and you’ll earn 5,000 RevPoints or Avios.

This number of points could, for example, get you a one-way flight with Aer Lingus to somewhere like London, Paris or Amsterdam.

Keep your credit card balance paid in full to avoid interest and charges and the reward flight will cost you the €30 stamp duty and the €17.99 a month in Revolut membership fees.

You can book an Avios reward flight through your airline loyalty account, such as AerClub, British Airways Club or Qatar Airways Privilege Club. You pay with Avios plus cash for taxes, fees and carrier charges.

When choosing a credit card don’t be blinded by the points. Weigh up the cost of the card, your capacity to keep the balance paid and how accessible the rewards really are.

If the scheme means spending more to earn a freebie, then it isn’t really free.

]]>AntonioGuillem<![CDATA[Consumers shopping for Christmas warned over fake listings and bogus delivery texts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/consumers-shopping-for-christmas-warned-over-fake-listings-and-bogus-delivery-texts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/consumers-shopping-for-christmas-warned-over-fake-listings-and-bogus-delivery-texts/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Fake listings and products that never arrive are the most common ways people are likely to be scammed in the run up to Christmas, with as many as a third of those who are duped being affected this way, research suggests.

A survey from digital bank Monzo found that bogus messages telling people they had missed parcel deliveries and phishing texts would be the next most-common scams to target Irish consumers in the coming weeks.

This is the most dangerous time for scams with 55 per cent of respondents saying they were more likely to purchase from retailers they had not used before in the run up to Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Christmas than during the rest of the year.

The research found that 69 per cent of consumers were more likely to trust a seller or business if they appeared to be based in Ireland.

About two-thirds (67 per cent) said they were more likely to trust someone who communicated in a friendly or familiar way, and 68 per cent admitted feeling awkward about asking someone to prove they were genuine.

“When something feels familiar, local or friendly, our brains take a shortcut and treat it as safe,” chartered psychologist Allison Keating said.

“That shortcut served us well when reputation was visible and dealings were face-to-face. But, online, familiarity can be used to exploit us.”

She said fake listings that copied well-known brands or phishing messages that used a supplier’s familiarity were “a mechanism to create trust, things we have encountered before feel safer and the halo effect means that one positive impression spills over into assumptions of honesty”.

Keating said this was known as a truth default. “We assume people are being honest, because everyday life would be unworkable otherwise, but scammers can take advantage of this,” she said.

“Most social norms discourage questioning someone’s honesty, so challenging a person feels rude and the fear of causing offence with that challenge is immediate and vivid while the financial loss feels abstract and unlikely.”

She said scams could “directly challenge how we see ourselves, leaving us feeling foolish and embarrassed that we didn’t spot it”.

]]>Sitthiphong<![CDATA[Irish Life in bid to build two hotels next to new US embassy in Ballsbridge]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/25/irish-life-in-bid-to-build-two-hotels-next-to-new-us-embassy-in-ballsbridge/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/25/irish-life-in-bid-to-build-two-hotels-next-to-new-us-embassy-in-ballsbridge/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Having secured planning permission in 2023 for a large-scale office scheme on the site of Hume House in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4, Irish Life has amended its plans for the property and is now aiming to develop two new hotels there instead.

The Irish Times understands that the company is currently in the advanced stage of negotiations with both Dalata Hotel Group and Staycity, in relation to the respective operation of the proposed hotels. A fully owned subsidiary of the Swedish-headquartered Scandic Hotels Group, Dalata operates the Clayton and Maldron brands in Ireland, while the Dublin-headquartered Staycity offers long-stay accommodation through the aparthotel model.

Any agreement with either of the parties to enter into a leasehold agreement for the hotels would be subject to Irish Life securing planning permission from Dublin City Council for their development. Located on Pembroke Road, the Hume House site is zoned Objective Z6 ‘Employment/Enterprise’ under the terms of Dublin City Council Development Plan 2022-2028, allowing specifically for “the creation and protection of enterprise” and “opportunities for employment creation”. The location of a hotel on the site is however “open for consideration” according to the development plan.

Irish Life’s negotiations with Dalata and Staycity follow on from its recent circulation through joint agents Savills and CBRE of a prospectus inviting hotel companies to submit their proposals for the operation of the proposed Hume House hotel scheme.

In a note covering the site’s potential, the agents highlighted a scheme designed by MCA Architects. Extending to a total area of about 16,000sq m (172,223sq ft) and distributed over 11 storeys (including basement), the development would, subject to planning permission, comprise either one hotel of 409 bedrooms or two separate hotels consisting of a 229-bedroom hotel and a 217-bedroom aparthotel.

Within both options, the proposed development would be laid out across two blocks, with an internal courtyard. The scheme would see the retention and repurposing of between 75 per cent and 80 per cent of the existing Hume House office building, which was built originally by G&T Crampton for the UK-based developer Hume Holdings in the 1960s.

Commenting on the potential market demand for the Pembroke Road hotels, Savills and CBRE said: “Once developed, we believe the Ballsbridge hotel opportunity will compete with hotels within close proximity, primarily in the four-star market.”

In the case of a single 409-bedroom hotel, they identified its competition as consisting of the following: the Clayton Hotel Ballsbridge; Clayton Hotel Burlington Road; Grand Canal Hotel; Herbert Park Hotel; InterContinental Dublin; Mespil Hotel and Sandymount Hotel.

‘Simply too large’: Ballsbridge locals object to proposed 10-storey hotel and aparthotel

The agents also considered the competition for Irish Life’s preferred development of a hotel and aparthotel on the site, and found it would also include a number of hotels operating in the extended-stay sector. These were: Beckett Locke; Premier Suites Dublin Ballsbridge; Premier Suites Dublin Leeson Street; Staycity Dublin Castle; Staycity Dublin City Centre; Staycity Mark Street, and Zanzibar Locke.

Irish Life’s current ownership of Hume House dates from 2016 when it purchased the building and its 0.35-hectare (0.86-acre) site for €35 million from Blackstone. The US private-equity giant had acquired the property for its part two years earlier as part of a €100 million deal with Nama for three of the four prime Dublin offices in the Platinum portfolio.

Irish Life had previously owned Hume House from the 1970s until 2006, when it sold it to developer Seán Dunne as part of a “swap” in which it was given ownership of Riverside IV, the newly developed headquarters of legal firm Matheson in Dublin’s south docklands. While the precise details of the transaction were never made public, the deal is understood to have valued each of the buildings at about €130 million at the time. Dunne acquired Hume House as part of his wider site assembly programme in Ballsbridge involving the adjacent Jurys and Berkeley Court hotels.

With the Jurys Hotel site now set to house the new US embassy and with the Berkeley Court Hotel already replaced by the Lansdowne Place apartment scheme, Irish Life will be hoping that Dublin City Council looks favourably on its plans to deliver additional hotel accommodation in Ballsbridge.

The news of Irish Life’s revised proposal for the Hume House site comes at the same time as the Irish Rugby Football Union is seeking a partner to design, build, finance and operate a new hotel and residential scheme immediately adjacent to the Aviva Stadium on Lansdowne Road in Dublin 4. Located next to the Lansdowne Road railway level crossing and directly opposite the entrance to the Aviva, the proposed Lansdowne Quarter is being envisaged as a 257-key hotel alongside a 77-unit residential apartment development.

Elsewhere in Ballsbridge, Renmark Property Holdings, a vehicle associated with Derek McGrath’s Core Capital, is currently seeking planning permission for a 244-bedroom hotel and an aparthotel with 194 rooms on the site of the former Zurich House at Ballsbridge Park, next to Meta’s European headquarters and across the road from the Merrion Road entrance to the RDS.

While the plans of Irish Life and the IRFU have yet to be submitted to Dublin City Council for its consideration, Renmark’s proposal has met with a degree of local opposition.

A complaint raised by several Ballsbridge residents was the perceived “overconcentration” of hotels in the area, with one local arguing that the area was a “residential neighbourhood and not a city-centre high street”.

Noting there were “three very large hotels” located nearby, they said “yet another hotel” would “exacerbate the existing saturation of hotel rooms within the immediate vicinity”.

]]><![CDATA[Emeis Ireland makes €54.4m loss as nursing home group ups staffing amid Hiqa inspections]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/emeis-ireland-makes-544m-loss-as-nursing-home-group-ups-staffing-amid-hiqa-inspections/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/emeis-ireland-makes-544m-loss-as-nursing-home-group-ups-staffing-amid-hiqa-inspections/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000French-owned nursing home group Emeis Ireland saw its net loss widen by almost 170 per cent last year as running costs soared amid a sharp increase in agency staffing, after the group faced healthcare watchdog inspections following an RTÉ Investigates programme on two of its homes.

Emeis Ireland’s loss jumped to €54.4 million in 2025 from €20.4 million for the previous year, the company said in newly-filed accounts with the Companies Registration Office.

Administration expenses spiralled 92 per cent higher to €66.6 million, with one of a number of driving factors understood to relate to an increase in agency staffing during 2025 as the company dealt with the fallout from the RTÉ programme.

The group, the biggest private nursing home provider in the State, was at the centre of controversy last year when the broadcaster highlighted allegations of staff shortages, elder abuse and neglect at two of its centres – The Residence in Portlaoise and Beneavin Manor in Dublin.

Following the broadcast, the Health Information and Quality Authority (Hiqa) commenced targeted inspections of nursing homes in the group and required the directors of the centres to take “urgent action with immediate effect to address the safety and wellbeing of residents”.

This is known to have led to Emeis increasing its reliance on agency staffing significantly. Emeis Ireland did not disclose the cost of agency staff in its accounts.

Separately, the company’s average number of employees increased by 9 per cent to 2,799 last year. Employee wages and salaries jumped almost 12 per cent to €88.7 million.

“The current employment environment in Ireland continues to pose challenges on the recruitment and retention of registered nurses and carers,” Emeis Ireland said in the report.

“The group has put in place a strong and experienced team to support recruitment and retention, and therefore the directors are of the opinion that the group is well positioned to manage this risk.”

What is Emeis and where are its Irish care homes located?

Paris-based Emeis, formerly known as Orpea, entered the Irish market in 2020 through the takeover of the TLC Nursing Home portfolio and followed up with further deals and home developments.

Emeis Ireland currently has 2,373 beds across 26 nursing homes. Unlike several overseas nursing home groups that have entered the market over the past seven years, the company owns most of its properties.

It had €559.9 million of loans from other parts of the wider group at the end of December, believed to largely relate to its property portfolio. Its interest bill last year amounted to €18.4 million. Seven of its properties are rented from third parties.

The company’s French parent required a bailout in 2023, led by a state-owned investment firm, in the wake of a scandal over residents’ mistreatment in its home market.

Hiqa published 54 inspection reports on 23 nursing homes run by Emeis Ireland in July of this year.

According to the inspection reports, a number of the centres were operating to a good standard and providing safe and effective care. However, seven centres were found to have “significant challenges in delivering safe and effective care”.

Emeis Ireland said after the publication of the reports that it worked closely with Hiqa throughout the process and has “implemented significant improvements across [its] nursing homes”.

It said it remained “fully committed to providing safe, high-quality care for all residents and will continue to work constructively with Hiqa to ensure these improvements are sustained”.

]]>Daniel Megias<![CDATA[Teneo’s Irish strategy and restructuring arms record higher profits]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/teneos-irish-strategy-and-restructuring-arms-record-higher-profits/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/25/teneos-irish-strategy-and-restructuring-arms-record-higher-profits/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 05:39:00 +0000The Irish arm of communications and advisory firm Teneo saw its profits increase by 1 per cent last year to just under €1 million, accounts show.

Its net fee income, however, declined by 8 per cent to €9.9 million, reflecting a different mix of clients and project work during 2025.

When the activities of a German affiliate called Herter are included, Teneo Strategy Ireland Ltd had revenues – which include costs incurred on behalf of clients – of €28.8 million and a net profit of just under €800,000. Herter’s revenue was €16 million among that total.

Teneo Strategy, including the German business, employed on average 95 staff last year. Between them, they received €13.5 million in wages and salaries, at an average of €142,382. Directors’ remuneration amounted to €525,653.

Recent new client wins on the strategy side in Ireland include Coca-Cola, Musgrave and Primark, which is known as Penneys in Ireland.

Other clients include Fáilte Ireland, Circle K, Toyota, Dublin Zoo, Bank of Ireland, Bord na Móna, British & Irish Lions, Aer Lingus and NFL.

Meanwhile, its sister company, Teneo Restructuring Ireland Ltd, which was set up in 2021 and is headed by Damien Murran, posted a net profit of €4.5 million on revenues of €11.6 million. A dividend of €1.86 million was paid to its owners.

In 2024, the restructuring business posted profit of €4 million on revenues of €8.8 million.

Teneo Restructuring employed on average 24 staff each month last year, with its bill for wages and salaries amounting to just under €4 million – an average of €165,000. Directors’ remuneration more than tripled to €1.45 million.

Teneo Ireland chief Mick O’Keeffe said its revenues for last year were “as planned and remained strong and stable after years of consistent and sustained growth”.

“It was also a year that focused on driving greater efficiency. Critically, as a mature and established business, we retained all our key clients and secured several new clients and mandates,” he said.

Murran said the restructuring unit continued to deliver “sustained profitable” growth.

“Key to success in the year was ongoing delivery from our core restructuring and insolvency team, which continued to deliver on some highly complex cases both domestically and internationally,” he said.

“We remain excited for the year ahead and have doubled down on our investment in the expansion of our services with several key hires already made in full year 2026 and more to follow early in ’27. Overall year-on-year headcount grew from 19 to 24 and currently stands at 32.”

Based in New York, Teneo was founded in 2011 and is led by global chief executive Paul Keary. Its Irish board is chaired by former Smurfit senior executive Gary McGann.

The firm recently worked on the stock market IPO of artificial intelligence company Anthropic on the Nasdaq exchange.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has issued an order for the National Development Bank (BGK) to provide financing for the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after Poland’s central bank froze the TK’s accounts following a disputed takeover of the court by government-backed judges.

The relevant funds for the TK to function will be allocated by the finance ministry, announced government spokesman Adam Szłapka on Thursday morning, a day after the cabinet approved a resolution authorising the move.

However, the ousted chief justice of the court has condemned the government’s actions as “completely unlawful” and said that they make the court’s current leadership “directly subordinate” to the prime minister.

Premier @DonaldTusk wydał dyspozycję, by Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego zapewniał finansowanie Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, a środki na ten cel zabezpieczy minister finansów. Państwo musi działać.

— Adam Szłapka (@adamSzlapka) November 26, 2026

The move marks the latest twist in a long-running battle for control over the TK, which dates back around a decade to the unlawful appointment to the court of three judges under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

As a result, Tusk’s centrist government, which took power from PiS in 2023, had effectively ignored the court and its rulings until this year, when it began appointing new judges to fill a growing number of vacancies on the TK’s 15-person bench.

Events came to a head on 30 October, when the eight judges appointed by Tusk’s majority in parliament – five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – seized control of the court.

They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under PiS, had been suspended. Święczkowski, backed by Nawrocki and PiS, rejected their actions as an illegal “coup d’état” and maintains he is the rightful head of the court.

 

The disputed status of the TK’s leadership led the National Bank of Poland (NBP) to announce earlier this month that it had frozen all outgoing transfers from TK accounts.

The central bank cited conflicting claims over who had the authority to manage the institution, saying it “has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal”.

The NBP is led by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under PiS and is a longtime associate of party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Tusk’s government condemned the bank’s decision as politically motivated and pledged to find alternative ways of securing the tribunal’s finances.

Meanwhile, both Święczkowski and Anna Korwin-Piątkowska, the government-backed judge who has assumed leadership of the court, each appealed to Glapiński to unblock the Constitutional Tribunal’s accounts and recognise their respective authority to manage the court’s funds.

Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026

On Wednesday, the government adopted a resolution “on taking measures necessary to prevent a crisis situation related to the functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal” due to the NBP’s decision to freeze its accounts.

“At a time when, after many years, an opportunity has arisen to overcome the constitutional crisis, restricting the Constitutional Tribunal’s ability to exercise its constitutional powers will negatively affect the level of legal certainty for individuals, including citizens,” the resolution reads.

It requires the prime minister and finance minister to take “appropriate measures to protect the interests of the State Treasury and to ensure the state’s internal security and public order.”

Szłapka subsequently announced that Tusk had instructed BGK, a state-owned development bank, to provide financing to the tribunal.

The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

Jan Grabiec, head of the prime minister’s chancellery, on Thursday morning told broadcaster TVN24 that the tribunal had an “auxiliary account” at BGK. This would allow its day-to-day operations to be financed despite the NBP’s decision to block payment orders, he added.

“It is not just a matter of ordinary tribunal staff potentially not receiving their salaries,” said Grabiec. “The State Treasury also bears responsibility for contracts entered into by the tribunal’s previous leadership that include specific payment deadlines.”

“This creates a liability for damages, potentially amounting to losses of many millions of zloty,” he added. “We cannot allow the State Treasury to be exposed to losses resulting from such politically motivated decisions of the National Bank of Poland.”

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

On Thursday, Święczkowski condemned the government’s decision to channel money to the TK through BGK, calling it “completely unlawful”, reports the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily.

“If this usurper Anna Korwin-Piotrowska accepts money from Tusk’s government, it will mean she is directly subordinate to Tusk,” he added.

At the time of writing, the NBP had not publicly commented on the government’s decision to channel funding to the tribunal through BGK. BGK, meanwhile, told PAP that it could not comment on the details of its arrangements with other parties, citing banking secrecy.

]]> Warsaw hospital accused of offering “VIP access” for politicians fined 2.3 million zloty https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/26/warsaw-hospital-accused-of-offering-vip-access-for-politicians-fined-2-3-million-zloty/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:33:33 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107534

The Warsaw hospital at the heart of a recent scandal over allegations that politically connected patients were given preferential treatment has been fined 2.3 million zloty (€520,000) after an investigation found that it admitted patients out of turn and doctors were absent during scheduled shifts.

The doctor at the centre of the scandal, who was a local councillor for Poland’s main ruling party, was charged with fraud in October and is now also facing disciplinary proceedings over alleged breaches of medical ethics and professional standards.

Niestety – Dawid K. jednak nie posiadł daru bilokacji, cudu nie było.

Z ustaleń kontrolerów Narodowego Funduszu Zdrowia wynika, że po prostu oszukiwał. Ale to nie jest tylko sprawa jednego młodego medyka z legitymacją Koalicji Obywatelskiej w torbie. Cały ten przypadek wiele… pic.twitter.com/DfC35LLUpo

— OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) November 26, 2026

The audit was conducted by the National Health Fund (NFZ), which finances public healthcare in Poland. It was carried out following a series of revelations in June by media outlets about alleged irregularities at the hospital.

Many of the claims centred around a young doctor, who can be identified only as Dawid K. under Polish privacy law due to the criminal proceedings against him. He served as coordinator of emergency services at the Southern Hospital.

News outlet Zero.pl was the first to report that the doctor, who also served as a local politician for the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that leads Poland’s ruling coalition, worked a seemingly impossible number of hours at four different hospitals and earned 1.6 million zloty last year alone.

The website alleged that the doctor had declared shifts when he was actually not present and cited instances in which he reportedly appeared in local media during hours when he was officially listed as being on duty at the hospital.

❗️ Błyskawiczne przyjęcia, wykonywanie pakietów kilkunastu, a nawet kilkudziesięciu badań w bardzo krótkim czasie, możliwość przebywania w innym pomieszczeniu niż ogół pacjentów. W Warszawskim Szpitalu Południowym stworzono nieoficjalnie szybszą i bardziej komfortową ścieżkę… pic.twitter.com/3aanpRVeBu

— Patryk Słowik (@PatrykSlowik) June 17, 2026

Over the following weeks, Zero.pl and two other news websites, Wirtualna Polska and Onet, revealed further alleged cases of huge salaries for some doctors and impropriety at the Southern Hospital, including preferential treatment for patients with political connections.

This included claims that there was a “VIP lounge” in which patients with connections to KO were given more comfortable facilities than others and that such patients were often allowed to skip the queue and receive treatment more quickly.

 

In its audit of the Southern Hospital, the NFZ found that certain patients had been admitted out of turn. Inspectors also identified cases in which patients in stable condition were admitted to the emergency department ahead of others whose health condition warranted more urgent attention.

The NFZ also found that doctors were absent during scheduled shifts and and that medical services were sometimes provided by staff without the required qualifications. The audit raised further concerns about the appointment of an inexperienced doctor as the coordinator of the emergency department.

In a statement published on Wednesday, the hospital acknowledged the NFZ’s fine but noted that it was a preliminary decision and that the hospital could submit objections. It said that its board was reviewing the details before deciding on its next steps.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

After announcing the end of its audit, the NFZ noted that it would forward the findings to prosecutors who have been investigating reports of irregularities at Southern Hospital.

Prosecutors last month charged Dawid K. with fraud, alleging that he submitted fraudulent or unreliable invoices to the hospital worth more than 583,000 zloty. He has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors are also investigating other cases of alleged wrongdoing at the hospital. However, a spokesman last month said that the findings so far do not confirm reports of a “VIP lounge” at the hospital.

Meanwhile, on Thursday, the spokesman for the National Chamber of Physicians (NIL), Poland’s medical professional body, announced that they had decided to bring disciplinary proceedings against Dawid K.

The claims against him concern alleged improper performance of medical duties, breaches of professional ethics, and conduct that undermined public trust in the medical profession.

Zgodnie z obietnicą przekazuję do wiadomości publicznej:

Rzecznik Odpowiedzialności Zawodowej podjął decyzję o przedstawieniu zarzutów Dawidowi K.

Dotyczą one rzetelności wykonywania zawodu, naruszenia etyki i podważenia zaufania do zawodu lekarza.

Będziemy informować o…

— Piotr Pisula (@PanPisula) November 26, 2026

In the wake of the allegations against him, Dawid K. resigned from his seat on the local council, left KO, and stopped working at the Southern Hospital. His former party also distanced itself from him.

Jan Grabiec, the prime minister’s chief of staff and head of the KO in the Mazovia province, which includes Warsaw, told reporters in June that the scandal “has no connection to KO, but since he was a KO councillor, we will be all the more stringent in holding those responsible to account”.

In July, the health minister, Jolanta Sobierańska-Grenda, unveiled a series of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in the healthcare system. They include caps on doctors’ salaries, a requirement for them to work at least half their statutory working time at a designated hospital, and a new electronic waiting list system.

Meanwhile, the mayor of Warsaw, Rafał Trzaskowski, who is also a deputy leader of KO, ordered a separate municipal audit of the hospital, which revealed a number of irregularities, including in relation to Dawid K.’s activities. It concluded with 44 recommendations that Trzaskowski said were being implemented.

]]> Poland plans no-fly zone on eastern border to aid downing of Russian missiles https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/25/poland-plans-no-fly-zone-on-eastern-border-to-aid-downing-of-russian-missiles/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:19:56 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107508

Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland’s defence ministry has announced plans to establish a no-fly zone along the country’s eastern border with the aim of making it easier to shoot down Russian missiles and drones that violate Polish airspace.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has again suggested that Poland should be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards the Polish border. However, the defence ministry acknowledged today that NATO is so far opposed to the idea.

Wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk zapowiedział wprowadzenie strefy zakazu lotów przy wschodniej granicy Polski.

Jak poinformował minister Tomczyk, rozporządzenie trafiło do rządowego zespołu, strefa ma obejmować od kilkunastu do 50 kilometrów przy granicy wschodniej Polski i ma… pic.twitter.com/3xF68uNNRU

— Dariusz Wiewiorka (@darekwiewiorka) November 25, 2026

Speaking on Wednesday at the opening of a new military satellite imaging centre, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that his department “will request the government to establish a no-fly zone on the country’s eastern border, to ensure Poland’s security”.

Tomczyk acknowledged that, after three Russian missiles struck southeastearn Poland last Friday, NATO had offered support, including the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland.

“But at the same time, the Polish military must do everything possible to protect our interests here and now,” he added.

The defence ministry recently took one such step by allowing easier identification of objects that can be shot down, said Tomczyk. “The no-fly zone at the state border will be an additional factor supporting the operations of the Polish Air Force.”

 

At a subsequent press briefing, Tomczyk provided more details of the plan. The proposed no-fly zone would stretch for a distance of between “a dozen or a few dozen kilometres from the border”, he said.

“When a Polish fighter pilot knows that an aircraft is entering Polish airspace from Ukraine, is flying at a certain altitude and speed, is entering the no-fly zone and is detected on radar, this constitutes grounds for shooting down such an object…We will also urge NATO as a whole to establish such a rule on the eastern flank.”

The deputy minister said that a relevant regulation had already been submitted and “will be processed in the coming weeks”. He expressed hope that the measures could be in place by the end of December or in early January.

As well as last Friday’s missile strikes, on Monday this week a Russian drone entered Poland from Ukraine and spent a few minutes in Polish airspace. The Polish military had been authorised to fire upon it, but eventually did not do so after it turned back towards the border.

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the "growing threat from Russia".

Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead https://t.co/foCWsBDazH

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 29, 2026

The government’s plans for a no-fly zone were, however, questioned by Mariusz Błaszczak, a former defence minister and now head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party.

Błaszczak noted that current regulations already allow the introduction of a temporary no-fly zone. He suggested that what the government had announced was simply a “cosmetic measure” and asked what “real operational capabilities” it would provide to the military.

Earlier on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported, based on unnamed sources, that Poland had, at a NATO meeting called on Monday to discuss last week’s Russian missile strikes in Poland, asked about the possibility of shooting down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards NATO states.

Asked about the issue, Tomczyk said that he could not confirm Bloomberg’s reporting, but noted that discussion of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine had been going on for months.

“NATO is not in favour of this in any way,” said Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. “If we want to make any decisions that concern the space over Ukraine, it must always be a decision of the entire NATO…Many months ago NATO decided that such a procedure was out of the question. And that’s where we stand now.”

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

On Wednesday morning, before Bloomberg’s report had been published, Sikorski, the foreign minister, was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio about the idea of shooting down missiles over Ukraine before they reached Poland.

“A missile or drone approaching our airspace already poses a direct threat to us, so I believe that shooting [it] down over Ukraine at Ukraine’s request would fall within the definition of self-defence,” said Sikorski. However, he acknowledged that any such policy would need to be agreed by NATO.

As far back as 2024, Poland proposed the idea of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory. But it was rejected by NATO, whose then-secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, said that it would risk NATO “becoming part of the conflict”.

]]> Warsaw orders protest outside constitutional court to end https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/25/warsaw-orders-protest-outside-constitutional-court-to-end/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:10:45 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=107499
