But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not.  The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents […]

The post OPINION: AI will favour the companies built for AI, not adapted to it appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> For decades, business leaders have been warned that the impending arrival of a new technology will completely reorder the corporate world. But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not. 

The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents aside.

With AI, however, the warning deserves more consideration. The reason is less to do with the technology itself, but rather who is best placed to use it, and that is increasingly becoming startups, rather than established companies. 

The web didn’t break incumbents

The common story of the web is that of upstarts bringing down giants, and the rankings seem to agree.

The world’s most valuable company in 1995 was a Japanese telephone operator. In the same year, Microsoft barely made number twenty on the list and Nvidia was just a startup.  Today Microsoft, Nvidia, Apple, Amazon and Alphabet lead the rankings, and just six of the largest companies in 1995 remain in the top thirty. 

Though on closer examination, the incumbents were not the disasters the ranking implies. 

Companies such as Exxon, Coca-Cola and Toyota, more than tripled their combined revenue between 1994 and 2024, meanwhile Microsoft grew more than fiftyfold. The web gave them access to better logistics, cheaper computing and wider reach.  Oil companies could use better software without becoming software companies. Carmakers could run a more efficient supply chain. And a wealthier world could buy more cars, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals. The incumbents benefited from the technologies that were supposed to be disrupting them. 

It is therefore unsurprising that business leaders often meet warnings about AI with scepticism.

Where AI goes further than the web

The businesses that didn’t survive the dawn of the web, such as film rentals and newspaper classifieds, were not simply slow to adapt, they were substituted. The web typically made companies more productive rather than redundant.  

AI shifts this balance. While early digitisation took information and transactions online, real people were still responsible for interpreting information, exercising judgement and making decisions. AI can now take on a substantial share of that work. This raises the question of substitution again, but this time for jobs that sit inside offices, rather than on high streets. 

The startup advantage

The existing structure of established companies is built around human specialisation. Different departments and systems to coordinate different skillsets. While this structure made scale possible, it now makes it difficult to rethink how work can be done, which is why simply introducing AI into existing roles can often fall flat.

Startups have the benefit of starting from scratch, they can design their business around AI from the outset. A small team can now do the work of hundreds, and the ones who remain can serve customers, handle expectations and set the direction of the business. 

In the web era, startups predominantly sold tools to incumbents. Today, startups can enter the same markets as established players, but with fewer layers and at a fraction of the cost. The difference is design, not effort. Hospitals, nurseries and restaurants will always need their existing structures, but if your employees are knowledge workers, AI can be the foundation for a far more efficient and cost effective company. 

What decides the contest

Incumbents have spent decades building their customer trust, brand, proprietary data and deep expertise. While these are incredibly valuable assets, they are merely a headstart, not a guarantee. 

The contest will now likely become one of speed. Startups have to earn trust and knowledge, and incumbents must rebuild how their organisation works. 

The second task may be more difficult. Startups can earn trust through transparency and delivering good work. For incumbents, the challenge is to dismantle a structure that employs and rewards the people they  have to depend on to change it. 

Build the company that replaces yours

Rather than looking for ways for AI to improve their current organisations, business leaders should instead ask how they would build them today, with no existing structure. 

Incumbents should not throw away what they have already built, but they can decide which parts add actual value. However, that is also to say the organisational architecture that implements those advantages are blocking a new way of working.

So the question now becomes; if you were starting from scratch today, how would you build a company designed to put yourself out of business?

Then find a way to build it first.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:14:18 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Why low-cost airline Gol is adding premium cabins to its Boeing 737s https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/low-cost-airline-gol-premium-cabin-boeing-737/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58077 Brazilian low-cost carrier Gol is sacrificing seat capacity across its Boeing 737 fleet to attract premium passengers - so what will travellers get for their fare?

The post Why low-cost airline Gol is adding premium cabins to its Boeing 737s appeared first on AGN.

]]> Brazilian airline Gol is introducing premium cabins across its narrowbody fleet for both domestic and international flights

The carrier revealed it will introduce a dedicated premium cabin on its Boeing 737-700, 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 aircraft from 15 February 2027. It will be called Gol Premium, and will take up the first three rows of each aircraft.

Six middle seats will be blocked from sale, leaving 12 available for booking.

The airline said the new premium cabin will be on domestic flights. It will also replace the existing premium economy seating on Gol’s international flights. Bookings for premium cabin seats open on 15 December.

What to expect from Gol’s new Boeing 737 premium cabin

There will be a curtain separating the premium cabin from economy. Passengers will enjoy their own overhead luggage space, priority boarding, and dedicated crew service onboard.

There will also be new catering options: including hot snacks, and a wider selection of drinks for passengers on longer domestic flights.

Those flying with Gol on international routes will also receive pillows, blankets and amenity kits.

“This transformation reinforces Gol’s commitment to continuously raising the standard of hospitality on board”, said Gol CEO Andre Fehlauer.

Will Gol install new premium seats?

Gol hasn’t announced plans to install wider premium seats. However, it has confirmed it will discontinue its Gol+Conforto seating category (premium economy).

Gol’s ambitions for 2027

As we recently reported, Gol has secured slots at London Gatwick airport, opening the possibility of non-stop flights from its base in Rio de Janeiro to the UK’s second busiest airport.

Gol has been awarded 372 of the 434 movements it requested for summer 2027. The allocation gives Gol capacity to operate around six weekly flights next year.

GOL has set its sights on an ambitious growth plan over the coming years after emerging from Chapter 11 restructuring.

The carrier is introducing the Airbus A330neo into its fleet, marking its foray into the widebody long-haul market. 

The Brazilian low-cost carrier plans to operate nonstop to New York, Orlando, Lisbon, and Paris from Rio de Janeiro.

It is currently using two leased Airbus A330-200s while it awaits the first deliveries of its five A330neos to be completed by the end of 2027. 

Speaking during the Routes Americas 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro earlier this year, former Gol CEO Celso Ferrer said that the carrier was looking to expand international routes beyond its traditional markets.

Why is a low-cost airline sacrificing seats?

For budget airlines, the business model is usually to fit more seats into an aircraft and maximise the number of passengers. By removing six seats from sale on its narrowbody fleet, Gol appears to be hoping the additional revenue from premium fares will outweigh the loss of economy tickets sales and the cost of providing an enhanced service.

Rival airline LATAM has offered a similar premium product with blocked middle seats on its domestic and regional narrowbody fleet since 2020.

Which other low-cost airlines are moving towards premium travel?

Gol is not the only budget carrier to embrace premium travel.

Earlier this month, the US Frontier Airlines opened bookings for its first-class seats on its Airbus narrowbody aircraft. Meanwhile fellow US budget carrier Allegiant Air is introducing eight first-class seats on selected aircraft from spring 2027.

And Wizz Air has taken a similar approach to Gol, introducing a ‘Wizz Class‘ seating option last year, with a guaranteed empty middle seat in the front row. And Germany’s Eurowings will start operating aircraft fitted with new Premium BIZ Seats on 1 December.

]]> Storms threaten busiest Thanksgiving skies in 16 years as US flight cancellations mount https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/thanksgiving-flight-cancellations-us-airports-2026/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:32:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58103 Severe weather is disrupting operations at major US airports, with airlines facing a race to recover their schedules ahead of Sunday's holiday travel rush.

The post Storms threaten busiest Thanksgiving skies in 16 years as US flight cancellations mount appeared first on AGN.

]]> Hundreds of flights have been cancelled across the United States on Thanksgiving Day as severe weather disrupts operations during what the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has forecast will be its busiest Thanksgiving period in 16 years.

As of 10:46 Eastern Time on 26 November, FlightAware data showed 396 flights within, into or out of the US had been cancelled, with a further 948 delayed.

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines have all issued travel waivers covering airports in the northeastern and mid-Atlantic states as a powerful storm moves along the East Coast.

The disruption comes after a difficult fortnight for US aviation, during which airlines and airports have grappled with a series of technical failures and operational incidents.

Thanksgiving storms hit major US airports

A coastal storm bringing heavy rain, flooding and strong winds to the northeastern US is affecting several major aviation hubs, including those serving New York, Boston and Washington DC.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has warned of significant disruption from storms affecting both US coasts over the Thanksgiving period.

Baltimore/Washington International Airport has been particularly badly affected, with around a quarter of its scheduled departures cancelled earlier on Thursday morning.

Other airports experiencing significant cancellations include New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport and LaGuardia Airport, as well as Boston Logan and Washington Reagan National.

Strong winds, reduced visibility and heavy rainfall can significantly reduce the number of aircraft airports are able to handle. Given the interconnected nature of US airline networks, disruption at major East Coast hubs could have implications for flights elsewhere in the country throughout the day.

Major US airlines issue Thanksgiving travel waivers

All four of the largest US airlines have introduced additional flexibility for passengers travelling through affected airports.

Delta Air Lines has issued a weather waiver covering nine airports, allowing eligible passengers to rebook their Thanksgiving flights for travel through 28 November without paying a fare difference, subject to certain conditions.

American Airlines has introduced flexibility covering the same nine airports, while United Airlines has issued a waiver covering seven airports across the region.

Southwest Airlines is also allowing affected passengers to change their travel arrangements, with a longer rebooking window of up to 14 days, according to TravelPulse.

While Thanksgiving Day itself is typically quieter than the days immediately preceding and following the holiday, airlines have been proactively cancelling flights to limit the operational impact of the storm.

A difficult fortnight for US aviation

The Thanksgiving disruption follows a series of technical problems that have exposed vulnerabilities in the US aviation system.

On 13 November, a communications outage prompted the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop lasting almost five hours, resulting in more than 18,000 flight cancellations and disrupting travel for more than one million passengers.

The FAA subsequently confirmed that the outage occurred following the installation of a new router at its telecommunications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

United Airlines and Delta Air Lines have also experienced separate technical outages in recent days.

Meanwhile, on Thanksgiving Eve, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 freighter overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport, temporarily forcing the closure of three of the airport’s four runways and prompting the FAA to issue a ground stop.

Neither pilot was injured in the incident, according to the Associated Press.

Busiest Thanksgiving skies in 16 years

Despite the recent disruption, the FAA is anticipating its busiest Thanksgiving period in 16 years, with more than 417,000 flights forecast over the nine-day holiday period.

Ahead of the travel rush, the agency established a dedicated team to manage potential disruption and expanded its use of technology designed to anticipate and mitigate airspace congestion.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) expects to screen around 17.6 million passengers between 24 and 30 November, according to Reuters.

Although slightly below last year’s passenger numbers, the busiest day of the holiday period is still to come. The TSA expects more than three million passengers to pass through airport security checkpoints on Sunday, 29 November, which would make it the busiest day for passenger screenings so far this year.

With adverse weather expected to continue affecting East Coast airports into Friday morning, airlines face the challenge of recovering their operations and repositioning aircraft and crews ahead of Sunday’s return travel rush.

]]> Why the USAF is spending $21 billion to modernise the B-52 bomber https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/b-52-100-years-service/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:41:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55880 Given the requirement for a high capacity delivery truck bomber and that any cleansheet bomber is decades away, upgrading the B-52H to the B-52J is the logical choice.

The post Why the USAF is spending $21 billion to modernise the B-52 bomber appeared first on AGN.

]]> Around 70 years after entering service in the early Cold War, the US Air Force is currently upgrading the Boeing B-52 fleet in an effort that may see it reach 100 years of USAF service.

While the programme may be shocking to the original engineers of the 1940s and 50s, the effort makes sense given the geopolitical realities, budget constraints, Air Force requirements, B-52 versatility, and various decisions with other bomber programmes that have been made along the way.

The B-52 was never intended to be a long-lived bomber

The famous WWII B-29 Superfortress bomber served the United States from 1944 to 1960.

The massive Convair B-36 Peacemaker entered service in 1948, and by 1956 it was being phased out and was completely retired in 1959, a period of around 11 years.

The Convair B-58 Hustler supersonic bomber entered service after the B-52, in 1960. Ten years later, it was likewise retired.

When it was developed and purchased by the Air Force, it had been assumed that the B-52 bomber would have an operational lifespan of 20 years, and would largely follow the course of its contemporary bombers.

The type entered service in 1955, and before the last units were delivered to the Air Force in 1962, the Air Force was already working on its replacement.

The B-52 was able to adapt to a changing environment

But the strategic environment changed in ways the Air Force had not anticipated and in ways that the B-52 found itself able to adapt to.

The development of ICBMs as the primary delivery weapon for nuclear weapons and the emergence of Soviet surface-to-air missiles were major contributing factors to cancelling the high-Mach, high-altitude XB-70 Valkyrie bomber.

The B-52 survived due to being surprisingly versatile (e.g., able to operate at low altitudes) and being the bomber that the Air Force already had when replacement bombers, including the original B-1A Lancer, were cancelled.

The development of the interim B-1B Lancer and purchase of 100 examples allowed the Air Force to thin its B-52 fleet and provide a stopgap for the much more ambitious stealth bomber programme that would culminate in the B-2 Spirit.

Separately, the B-1B’s story echoes the B-52, although it is less dramatic. It was originally intended to have an operational life of as little as 10 years.

The B-1B’s service life has been influenced by several factors, including the reduced B-2 procurement, changing force requirements, and subsequent retirement decisions.

The latest budget documents suggest the Lancer is now set to serve until 2037.

The niche opened up by stealth bombers

Paradoxically, expensive, high-end, but payload-constrained (by internal bays) bombers like the B-2 and incoming B-21 create a need for a missile truck.

Not every mission requires a high-end stealth bomber, and sometimes the skies are permissive enough for a vulnerable, but relatively cheap and high-payload bomber, like the B-52, to operate.

More importantly, the future of air combat is seeing the development of an increasingly large portfolio of ultra-long-range munitions that can be launched from outside contested airspace.

This is the primary role that the Air Force is keeping the B-52 on for. It complements the B-21 outside of contested airspace as well as serving in a nuclear deterrence role.

The upgrade to the B-52J variant

The B-52H fleet is now old, and the type’s engines are in need of replacement. The Air Force is currently working to upgrade them to the new B-52J variant through the Commercial Engine Replacement Program (CERP).

An article by the government watchdog, GAO, writes, “The Air Force plans to spend $21 billion modernizing the remaining 70-plus active B-52s. This plan is one of the most extensive modernization programs in Air Force history.”

Not only will this provide them with new Rolls-Royce F130 engines, but it will also deliver new avionics, better networking, and the ability to carry future high-end missiles.  In total, there are 13 modernization efforts underway.  

Currently, the Air Force expects the first upgraded B-52J bomber to enter service in 2033 and serve into the 2050s.

As in the past, the Air Force is in the position that it needs a heavy payload bomber to complement the B-21 fleet. However, it would likely take decades to design, test, field, and mature such a bomber should the effort start today.

Although future concepts for a B-52 successor continue to be discussed, no replacement is currently close to entering service.

Until then, the Air Force needs to rely on its existing fleet. The B-1B Lancer fleet increasingly worn out and is already difficult to maintain, while the B-2 is fundamentally the wrong aircraft for the role and exists in low numbers.

The size, versatility, and remaining flight hours of the B-52 make it the Air Force’s default choice.

]]> When Norwegian Air gave up long-haul flying during its bankruptcy restructuring, Norse Atlantic saw an opportunity to keep low-cost flights across the Atlantic alive. 

Some of the people behind the new airline had held senior roles at Norwegian. They still saw a market for those flights, and Norwegian’s former Boeing 787 Dreamliners gave them a fleet to launch with.

But Norse found the low-cost long-haul market just as challenging as every airline that has gone before. It struggled to make a profit, and turned to flying services on behalf of other carriers in an attempt to make money.

Norse tried and failed at low-cost long-haul

Norse launched commercial operations in June 2022, flying from Oslo to New York and later adding services from London Gatwick to New York as well.

Everything was set for success. The aircraft were available on favourable lease terms, and as the world emerged from the pandemic disruption, there were a few gaps in the long-haul market that Norse hoped to fill.

But fuel prices were high, and this thin schedule meant aircraft were underutilised. This manifested in a first-year net loss of $175 million in 2022.

Nevertheless, Norse pressed ahead with its expansion in 2023, establishing a UK subsidiary in March and growing London Gatwick to its largest base. By summer ‘23, Norse was flying to seven US cities from Gatwick: New York, Orlando, Fort Lauderdale, Washington DC, Boston, Los Angeles and San Francisco. 

But even before the year was out, signs were pointing to a hasty retreat from these highly competitive routes. San Francisco, Boston and Washington were withdrawn, while Fort Lauderdale was repointed to Miami. Norse attempted to diversify, adding flights to Caribbean destinations including Jamaica and Barbados for the winter season.

Although it did have one profitable quarter during the summer of 2023, it ended the year with a net loss of $168.6 million.

Through 2024, Norse continued to experiment, adding Las Vegas and Cape Town from Gatwick. However, the Caribbean routes did not return for the winter. The airline continued to increase its overall revenue, but still ended the year loss-making.

Flying for other airlines offered Norse a lifeline

Operating services on behalf of other airlines was part of the Norse plan from the outset. As early as March 2022, it agreed to sublease four surplus Boeing 787s to Air Europa on a dry lease basis. It was November that year before it started operating ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance) services for other carriers.

By 2024, ACMI had become one of the strongest parts of the Norse business, augmented with a deal with Indian low-cost airline IndiGo to provide six of its Boeing 787s for European services – half the available fleet.

The IndiGo deal was intended to be a turning point for Norse, offering predictable, year-round income, reduced exposure to fuel price volatility and a means of monetising the aircraft it was still paying to lease but not otherwise flying.

The phased introduction of the Norse aircraft took all of 2025. The fifth aircraft joined in December, and the sixth only began flying for IndiGo in January this year. Nevertheless, the ACMI work saw Norse grow its annual revenue by 128% in 2025, including charter customers and one-off flights.

But the bottom line was still raw. High costs of aircraft operations and pressure to keep fares low meant that even when its aircraft were full, it was struggling to make any money. 2025 ended with a smaller, but still substantial, $61.9 million loss.

2026 should have been a great year for Norse Atlantic

This year started strongly for Norse, with six of its Dreamliners contracted to IndiGo and a new plan to operate its own flights on underserved routes to Thailand. 

It had launched services from Gatwick to Bangkok in October 2025, adding Manchester to Bangkok later in the year. In tandem, it was operating a handful of routes from Oslo and Stockholm to Thai destinations too. Thailand was seen as a golden opportunity for the airline, with few to no competing nonstop flights and plenty of demand for the services.

When IndiGo said it would be returning the first Dreamliner to Norse in June, the airline took it in its stride, announcing that “With the additional aircraft, we look forward to deploying extra capacity on our successful and profitable Thailand routes.”

Two weeks later, Norse announced an expanded Thailand winter programme, including a new Gatwick-Phuket service and quadrupling Manchester-Bangkok frequencies.

All this came despite the surging cost of aviation fuel, caused by the conflict in Iran, and various airspace restrictions affecting flight paths for many of its competitors. The airline said specifically that its Thailand services were using a northerly air corridor and were therefore unaffected by airspace issues.

The dream of Norse Atlantic unravels

Despite the chipper start to the year, Norse did not have a good 2026. High fuel prices meant it was operating its own services on wafer-thin margins, and even with the ACMI revenue, it ended the first half of the year with an almost $100m loss.

The hardest blow came at the end of July, when IndiGo revealed it would be terminating all services with Norse. The reasons given were elevated fuel prices, airspace disruption and the longer routings between India and Europe. IndiGo said this had undermined the profitability of its long-haul plans.

For IndiGo, the Dreamliners had always been an interim solution, allowing it to establish a European presence and gain long-haul operational experience ahead of the delivery of its own widebody Airbus A350s. As it began taking delivery of its A321XLRs, it chose to focus on routes it could fly with its own metal, removing one of the Nordic airline’s biggest sources of income.

That contract officially ended on 1 November. The airline had a small reprieve via a deal with Pakistan International Airlines to operate two of its Dreamliners for routes into Europe. But occupying two 787s doesn’t pay for the rest. 

At the end of 2025, Norse still had almost $780 million in outstanding lease liabilities, with aircraft lease terms extending years into the future. High overheads, low income and a difficult aviation market have all led to the predicament we see today.

Norse Atlantic has never made an annual profit

Despite one profitable quarter, the annual result from Norse’s operations has always been a negative.

Source: Norse Atlantic annual reports and interim financial results. All figures in US dollars.

What’s next for Norse Atlantic?

Norse Atlantic has not yet filed for bankruptcy, but its decision to suspend all flights on 26 November suggests the airline has exhausted its immediate financial options. 

The company remains in discussions with potential investors over a takeover that would include a financing solution, although it has warned that bankruptcy proceedings will follow if emergency funding cannot be secured.

Even if a buyer can be found, it is difficult to envisage Norse returning in its current form. A smaller operation focused on charter and wet-lease services, potentially retaining some of its more lucrative leisure routes, could offer a more sustainable business model. 

However, having accumulated losses of more than $635 million by the middle of 2026, Norse’s predicament serves as another reminder of just how difficult it is to make low-cost long-haul aviation work, even with modern, fuel-efficient aircraft and strong passenger demand.

]]> SpaceX cleared to deploy a million AI satellites as Musk looks towards a Kardashev Type II civilisation https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/fcc-approves-spacex-starmind-1-million-ai-satellites/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:02:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58027 The US FCC has approved SpaceX’s Starmind project to deploy up to one million solar-powered AI satellites in orbit.

The post SpaceX cleared to deploy a million AI satellites as Musk looks towards a Kardashev Type II civilisation appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorised SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) computing hardware, paving the way for what could become the largest satellite constellation ever assembled.

The approval, announced on 25 November, lets SpaceX proceed with its Starmind project, which aims to use solar energy collected in orbit to power space-based data centres and transmit the results of their computations back to Earth.

The US regulator has granted the first authorisation for a constellation of orbital data centres, amid growing concerns over the availability of electricity, land and water to support the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure on Earth.

However, SpaceX founder and chief executive Elon Musk has a much larger ambition for the project, one rooted in a scientific theory proposed by a Soviet astronomer more than six decades ago.

Musk sees orbital data centres as an early step towards humanity becoming a Kardashev Type II civilisation, a hypothetical society capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its host star.

The FCC itself referred to the concept in announcing its decision as its chairman Brendan Carr said, “More fundamentally, it ( the constellation of data centres in space) promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun.”

“This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” Carr said, adding, “Compute campuses or data centres are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centres are meeting the moment.”

SI, or superintelligence, refers to artificial intelligence that would surpass human intellectual capabilities.

The regulator said the system also operates consistent with the FCC’s orbital debris rules, and that it is continuing to assess other proposals for orbital data centres.

What is SpaceX’s Starmind project?

Unlike SpaceX’s Starlink satellites, which primarily provide communications and internet connectivity, Starmind spacecraft are designed to process data in orbit.

Each satellite would effectively function as a small data centre, carrying computer processors, solar arrays, communications equipment and a system to dissipate the heat generated by its electronics.

Multiple satellites would be connected through high-speed optical links, allowing them to exchange information using lasers. Starlink would provide the communications network through which the results of AI computations could be transmitted back to users on Earth.

SpaceX has already unveiled its AI1 satellite design, which draws on technologies developed for its Starlink constellation.

According to specifications published by SpaceX, the spacecraft will feature a 210kW solar array with a power generation density of 250 watts per square metre. The solar technology is being manufactured by SpaceX in Bastrop, Texas.

The company has also designed the spacecraft to accommodate computing modules from different chip manufacturers, allowing it to take advantage of advances in semiconductor technology without being tied to a single supplier.

SpaceX is building a dedicated manufacturing facility, called Gigasat, in Bastrop. The company expects the facility to support the production and deployment of thousands of AI satellites starting as early as late 2027.

Why does SpaceX want to move data centres into space?

The expansion of AI has created a growing demand for electricity. Large terrestrial data centres require substantial amounts of power to operate their processors and cooling equipment. They also need land, access to electricity networks and, depending on their cooling systems, considerable quantities of water.

SpaceX believes it can overcome some of these constraints by moving the computing infrastructure into orbit, where solar energy can be collected without interference from clouds or the Earth’s atmosphere.

The company intends to operate its AI satellites in sun-synchronous orbits. These are orbits in which a satellite passes over locations on Earth at approximately the same local solar time. Carefully selected orbital configurations can provide near-continuous exposure to sunlight.

Cooling, however, presents a different engineering challenge in space.

Although the surrounding environment is cold, the absence of air means that heat cannot be carried away from electronic equipment through convection. Satellites instead rely on radiators to release waste heat as infrared radiation.

SpaceX claims its approach could reduce the power required for cooling by a factor of 10 compared with conventional terrestrial data centres.

The FCC authorisation also allows SpaceX to use radiofrequency communications as a backup to its optical network. Separate radio links will support emergency communications, spacecraft tracking and command functions.

What is the Kardashev scale?

In 1964, Soviet radio astronomer Nikolai Kardashev published a scientific paper titled Transmission of Information by Extraterrestrial Civilizations.

At the time, astronomers were investigating whether signals from technologically advanced extraterrestrial societies could be detected from Earth.

Kardashev approached the question by considering how much energy such civilisations might have at their disposal. The greater their energy resources, the more powerful their potential communications systems could be.

His classification subsequently became known as the Kardashev scale. In its widely used modern interpretation, it divides civilisations into three broad categories.

A Type I civilisation would be capable of exploiting energy resources on a planetary scale. In Earth’s case, this would encompass energy received from the Sun as well as other available resources.

A Type II civilisation would have access to the entire energy output of its host star, requiring infrastructure extending far beyond its home planet.

A Type III civilisation would be capable of harnessing energy on the scale of an entire galaxy, potentially drawing power from billions of stars.

American astronomer Carl Sagan subsequently refined the classification in the 1970s by introducing intermediate values, according to Britannica.

Why Musk wants to capture a millionth of the Sun’s energy

The Sun produces approximately 3.8 x 1026 W of power. Earth intercepts less than one two-billionth of that output, and humanity currently uses only a small fraction of the solar energy that reaches the planet.

Capturing even one-millionth of the Sun’s total output would provide approximately 380 trillion kilowatts of power, more than 1,000 times the total solar power intercepted by Earth.

Musk has used this comparison to illustrate the potential scale of energy generation beyond the planet.

“Our progress toward a Kardashev Type II civilisation, let’s have an aspiration that if we say that our goal is to get even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, that would be more than 1,000 times as much energy as could possibly be produced on Earth,” Musk said.

The Starmind project would operate on a considerably smaller scale.

The Starmind doesn’t envisage transmitting electricity back to Earth. The energy would be consumed by the spacecraft themselves.

Starship critical to SpaceX’s orbital data centre ambitions

Much of SpaceX’s ability to realise the Starmind project will depend on Starship, the company’s heavy-lift launch vehicle designed to be fully reusable.

Deploying one million satellites would require manufacturing and launch capabilities far beyond those currently available to the global space industry.

To put the number into perspective, approximately 28,800 satellites have been launched since the beginning of the space age in 1957, through about 7400 rocket launches, till early this year, according to figures cited by the European Space Agency (ESA).

SpaceX is targeting the third quarter of 2027 for the first Starmind satellite launches, according to reports.

SpaceX is also facing competition. Google, Starcloud, Blue Origin and Cowboy Space are among the companies exploring space-based computing. Google and Starcloud have already launched experimental AI satellites.

]]> NASA deploys P-3 Orion, Gulfstream III and King Air to monitor Iowa lead azide detonation https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nasa-research-aircraft-iowa-lead-azide-detonation/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:13:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57987 NASA mobilized three airborne research aircraft - a Lockheed P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III, and a Beechcraft King Air B200 - alongside its TEMPO satellite to collect atmospheric data during the US Army’s controlled detonation of 4.5 metric tonnes of unstable lead azide in Middletown, Iowa.

The post NASA deploys P-3 Orion, Gulfstream III and King Air to monitor Iowa lead azide detonation appeared first on AGN.

]]> NASA deployed three of its airborne research aircraft to Iowa this week to collect atmospheric and environmental data as the US Army carried out the controlled detonation of nearly 4.5 metric tonnes of unstable explosive material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.

A Lockheed P-3 Orion and a Gulfstream III from NASA’s Langley Research Center in Virginia were joined by a Beechcraft King Air B200 contracted by the agency’s Ames Research Center in California.

NASA also drew on observations from its space-based Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) instrument as part of a coordinated federal response to the operation on 25 November.

The US Army had identified approximately 4,400kg of degraded lead azide that had become unstable during storage. The disposal operation raised concerns about the potential release of airborne lead particles.

A US Army spokesman said: “Today’s successfully controlled detonation exceeded expectations. Credit goes to our EOD professionals and the Soldiers on the ground today, with every indication showing the munitions used substantially reduced the lead azide threat and safely addressed the hazard. “

They added there was a reading of 0.0 lead detected on the ground after the detonation, explaining: “Immediate overhead coverage after the operation confirmed that everything targeted for removal was cleared, with no secondary explosions, no kickout, and no infrastructure damage on or around the installation.”

However, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said its air monitoring equipment had detected no airborne lead before, during or immediately after the detonation.

“All EPA air monitors continue to report a ZERO DETECT of airborne lead, which has remained consistent before, during, and after this morning’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant,” the agency said.

Around 300 EPA personnel were involved in collecting air, soil and water samples across the region. More than 1,200 samples had been collected before the detonation, with further samples being sent to laboratories for analysis.

NASA said it had “rapidly mobilized specialized research aircraft, space-based observation capabilities, and scientific personnel” to support the operation.

The deployment brought together three very different aircraft types, ranging from a 60-year-old former naval patrol aircraft to a converted business jet and a twin-engine general aviation turboprop.

All three types have been used extensively in airborne scientific research.

NASA’s 60-year-old P-3 Orion flying laboratory

The largest of the three aircraft deployed to Iowa is a former US Navy P-3 Orion built in 1966. Registered N426NA and designated NASA 426, the aircraft entered the agency’s airborne science programme in 1991.

Developed from the Lockheed L-188 Electra commercial airliner, the four-engine turboprop was designed for maritime patrol and anti-submarine warfare. Its long endurance and ability to operate at relatively low altitudes also made it suitable for atmospheric research.

NASA has used the aircraft to study weather systems, atmospheric chemistry, oceans, glaciers and polar ice. It also serves as a test platform for instruments being developed for future satellite missions.

The Orion has undergone extensive modifications since leaving military service. Openings have been incorporated into the upper and lower fuselage, allowing scientific instruments to make upward and downward-looking observations.

Seven cabin windows have been adapted to accommodate externally mounted experiments, while additional equipment can be fitted to the nose, tail and 10 mounting points on the wings.

Even the aircraft’s former weapons bay has found a new purpose. It can accommodate large scientific sensors and antennas or be configured to release atmospheric measuring devices known as dropsondes.

These instruments collect information on temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure and wind as they descend.

The P-3 can remain airborne for up to 12 hours, depending on its payload and weather conditions. It has a range of 3,800 nautical miles (7,038km), a useful payload of approximately 8,165kg and can accommodate up to 24 people, including its flight crew.

Despite its age, the aircraft has modern avionics and satellite communications equipment. Scientists can access meteorological information and aircraft position data during flight, while the communications network allows them to exchange information with other aircraft and ground teams.

Gulfstream III: From military transport to atmospheric research

NASA’s Gulfstream III also began its operational life as a military aircraft. In September 2017, NASA received authorisation to acquire three surplus C-20B Gulfstream III aircraft from the US Air Force. Two were allocated to support the agency’s spare parts requirements, while the third was assigned to scientific research.

The research aircraft, registered N520NA and designated NASA 520, arrived at Langley in December 2017, replacing the agency’s Dassault HU-25A Guardian.

The twin-engine business jet can accommodate a range of instruments designed to examine atmospheric composition and measure the distribution of airborne particles.

Among the instruments compatible with the Gulfstream III is NASA’s High-Altitude Lidar Observatory (HALO), which uses laser pulses to obtain information about water vapour, methane, clouds and aerosols beneath the aircraft.

Another instrument, the second-generation High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL-2), allows scientists to examine the distribution and optical properties of airborne particles and clouds.

Unlike instruments that require an aircraft to fly directly through the air being sampled, lidar can make measurements remotely. Scientists can use the returning laser signals to establish how particles are distributed at different altitudes.

The Gulfstream III can also accommodate instruments that analyse the chemical composition of aerosols and measure individual soot particles.

NASA has not disclosed the precise combination of scientific instruments carried aboard the aircraft during the Iowa deployment.

Beechcraft King Air B200: A versatile research aircraft

The smallest aircraft involved in the operation was a Beechcraft King Air B200 operating under contract to NASA’s Ames Research Center.

The King Air 200 family dates back to the early 1970s, with the prototype making its first flight in October 1972. The B200 subsequently introduced more powerful engines and improved performance.

Widely used for business aviation, cargo transport and medical evacuation, the aircraft family also serves with the US military as the C-12 Huron utility transport.

NASA has been using B200 aircraft since the early 1980s, adapting them for a variety of aeronautical and environmental research programmes.

Its own modified King Air aircraft feature openings in the cabin floor through which cameras, radar equipment and laser-based instruments can make observations of the atmosphere, land or water below.

NASA’s Langley-based B200, for example, has additional mounting points beneath its wingtips for instruments that sample airborne particles.

A separate B200 operated by NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center has supported research into ocean circulation, soil moisture, snow cover and airflow over aircraft wings.

The relatively small size of the King Air makes it a practical choice for research missions that do not require the payload capacity or endurance of larger aircraft.

NASA has not identified the registration or detailed scientific configuration of the contracted B200 deployed to Iowa.

Monitoring air pollution from space

Complementing the three aircraft was NASA’s TEMPO instrument, which observes atmospheric pollution across North America from geostationary orbit.

Its measurements from geostationary orbit of ozone, aerosols, and clouds can create a dataset that provides understanding and improve prediction of air quality and physical risks on climate.

Unlike Earth observation satellites that pass over a particular location periodically, TEMPO can repeatedly observe the same geographical region throughout daylight hours.

Its measurements include nitrogen dioxide, ozone and formaldehyde, providing scientists with information about changes in atmospheric pollution.

Airborne instruments can supplement these observations by examining atmospheric conditions in greater detail over a specific area.

NASA has yet to release the scientific findings from its Iowa flights or specify the individual assignments undertaken by the three aircraft.

Jared Isaacman defends NASA’s involvement

NASA’s deployment also prompted an unusual exchange between the agency’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and former US Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene.

Greene questioned NASA’s involvement on social media, compared the planned detonation to the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and disputed the Apollo Moon landings.

Isaacman dismissed the comparison, pointing out that the Iowa operation involved the controlled disposal of ageing explosive material rather than a nuclear reactor accident.

“In challenging circumstances such as this, you want the nation’s best on the field,” Isaacman wrote. “That is precisely why you call on NASA, putting our airborne and space-based sensors and some of the brightest scientific minds in the country to work.”

He also responded to Greene’s remarks about the Apollo programme.

“And we did go to the Moon,” Isaacman wrote. “It is disheartening that this needs to be explained to a former member of Congress.”

]]> Could a 2,000 ft altitude change transform aviation’s climate impact? UK researchers think so https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/contrail-avoidance-2000-ft-operation-blue-skies/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 10:55:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=58004 Cambridge researchers say a 2,000 ft change in cruising altitude could help flights avoid the most climate-warming contrails.

The post Could a 2,000 ft altitude change transform aviation’s climate impact? UK researchers think so appeared first on AGN.

]]> University of Cambridge researchers say climbing or descending by around 2,000ft could let some flights avoid forming persistent contrails. These ice clouds account for a substantial share of aviation’s warming. 

The researchers set out a plan to make such adjustments routine in UK-administered airspace in a policy briefing released during COP31 on 18 November.

The Aviation Impact Accelerator (AIA) estimates that 2–5% of flights cause 80–90% of contrail warming. Airlines would only need to adjust the flights forecast to produce the most warming, and the researchers say around 2,000 ft in either direction would be enough in most cases.

Why 2,000 ft can make a difference

Contrails form when water vapour in hot exhaust meets sufficiently cold air and freezes into ice crystals. In drier air, the crystals disappear quickly. In cold, humid layers, they can survive for hours and spread into thin clouds. Those clouds can reflect sunlight, but they also trap heat. Their net effect depends on where and when they form.

A flight can pass above or below one of those layers without changing its destination or making a long diversion. The difficulty is accurately forecasting the layer’s depth and position, then finding an alternative flight level that air traffic controllers can clear.

Cambridge estimates that targeted avoidance could increase fuel burn by about 0.1% averaged across an airline’s fleet. An individual flight could burn more if it leaves its most efficient cruising level. 

The authors argue that avoided warming can outweigh the extra CO₂ on carefully selected flights. They estimate that avoiding persistent contrails could almost halve aviation’s climate impact, though the outcome depends on forecast accuracy and how widely avoidance can be used.

Eliot Whittington, Cambridge Institute for Sustainable Leadership, said: “Aeroplane contrails significantly warm our planet, but the science and technology of how we can stop this is getting increasingly clear. We need to be prepared with practical routes to implement contrail avoidance at scale as soon as we’ve successfully completed the necessary trials, which is why we developed this policy brief. This is one of the simplest and easiest actions we can take on climate change, and we’ve found that there’s a huge amount of willingness from industry and regulators to act on a well-designed plan. The key will be making sure there is clear leadership and commitment to drive this forward.” 

What Operation Blue Skies will test

As ADS Advance reported in August, the UK’s Operation Blue Skies also aims to reduce contrails by adjusting aircraft altitude. The £5 million, 30-month programme includes £2.65 million from the Department for Transport. 

Its flight trials are scheduled for the winters of 2026–27 and 2027–28 in Shanwick oceanic airspace over the eastern North Atlantic. NATS expects about 20–40 test days each winter, during periods of lighter traffic. Modelling cited by NATS puts Shanwick’s share of global contrail warming at around 5%.

Google is developing AI models to flag where warming contrails are likely to form and using satellite imagery to help assess what happened. The Met Office is developing a contrail forecast capability. 

NATS will coordinate altitude changes using normal air traffic control procedures, and researchers at Imperial College London and Cambridge will evaluate the results. The programme will assess whether the changes can be made safely in regular traffic and whether they deliver a measurable climate benefit.

From winter trials to routine flight planning

The roadmap calls for the Met Office to make contrail forecasts available as standard aviation data and for flight-planning software to use them to propose workable alternatives before departure. Cambridge also suggests a fee and rebate tied to existing airspace charges, with a possible start in Shanwick from 2030.

“Contrail avoidance represents one of the most exciting opportunities we have to halve aviation’s climate impact. By making small adjustments to just a fraction of flights, we have the potential to make a very significant difference to global warming, quickly and at remarkably low cost,” Dr Samuel Gabra, Director, Aviation Impact Accelerator, said in the Cambridge announcement of its report, describing it as “a practical policy pathway to make this happen.”   

“The UK has a unique opportunity to lead the world in turning this science into action,” Gabra added. “Operation Blue Skies is an important first step, but our ambition must be much bigger: to make contrail avoidance routine across UK airspace and ultimately around the world.”

]]> Ukraine reports five Russian MiG-31s and Su-34s struck at Savasleyka https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/ukraine-claims-five-russian-fighters-hit/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 09:47:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57977 If confirmed, the reported strike could represent a notable hit to Russia's modern combat aircraft fleet, although the extent of any damage remains unclear.

The post Ukraine reports five Russian MiG-31s and Su-34s struck at Savasleyka appeared first on AGN.

]]> Another five Russian combat aircraft may have been damaged or destroyed on the ground in the latest Ukrainian strike, according to reports. If true, the strikes add to mounting losses for Russian warplanes on the ground in recent months.

Videos purporting to show burning MiG-31s and Su-34s have circulated online, but their authenticity could not be independently verified.

No verified satellite images have yet been released.

Ukraine claims to have hit another five Russian fighters

Yesterday, the Ukrainian General Staff reported having destroyed five Russian fighters at the heavily defended Savasleyka Airfield. It said, “According to preliminary information, three russian MiG-31s and two Su-34s were hit and will be unable to fly for some time.”

The MiG-31 Foxhound interceptor is regarded as the world’s fastest in-service fighter jet, while the Su-34 is a fighter-bomber heavily used for glide-bomb attacks. Neither is a multirole fighter.

Ukraine added that the extent of the damage and the exact number of aircraft struck are still being verified, while adding “there may be even better news to come.”

The BBC also reported on the strike, but largely repeated the same Ukrainian report.

Savasleyka Airfield is where Russian MiG-31 interceptors take off carrying high-Mach Kinzhal missiles used to strike Ukrainian cities.

If the Ukrainian claim that five Russian fighters were rendered inoperable, the losses would amount to roughly 1% of some estimates of Russia’s modern fighter inventory.

A bad streak for Russian combat aviation

The reported strike follows Russia’s loss of around 13 combat aircraft in October, including up to six Su-34s in a single strike and a Su-34 and Su-35 in another.

In November, another three helicopters were reported by Russian sources as shot down over St. Petersburg due to friendly fire, and a Russian Navy Ka-27 helicopter was reportedly destroyed with its Merkury corvette in Libya.

Ukraine has also teased to have damaged or destroyed three unspecified Sukhoi aircraft last week, but no evidence has emerged. Additionally, Ukraine has damaged or destroyed a Russian Il-76 strategic transport on the ground.

AGN has reported on a steady stream of new fighter deliveries to the Russian Air Force. These appear to be enough to sustain the core fighter jet fleet, but arguably not the wider fleet suffering from combat losses, mishaps, wear and tear, and general obsolescence.

Russia has been modernizing Soviet-era MiG-31s to the MiG-31BM/BSM/K variants. At the start of 2026, the think tank Rusi estimated Russia had 125-130 examples in inventory.

The OSINT analyst Jakub Janovsky estimated Russia may have around 64 operational, alongside around 140 operational Su-34s. Overall, he estimated Russia’s modern fighter fleet to be around 475 aircraft, excluding dated types like MiG-29s and Su-27s.

Rusi estimated around 560 modern fighters, largely due to higher MiG-31 numbers.

Six Russian Su-34s reportedly destroyed or damaged in Ukrainian strike Six Russian Su-34s reportedly destroyed or damaged in Ukrainian strike

Russia’s combat aircraft losses

The closely watched Russian Telegram account, Fighter-Bomber, did not confirm or deny the MiG-31 and Su-34 strikes. Fighter-Bomber is an account run by the retired Russian Su-34 pilot called Ilya Tumanov.

Instead, he posted, “If we divide aviation losses into categories, the picture looks like this: – 40% – aircraft destroyed on the ground – 30% – accidents for various reasons, plus airframe life exhaustion – 10% – friendly fire – 20% – enemy air defence.”

He then added jokingly, “Of course, this isn’t happening to us. I have no idea where it is happening, though.”

Tumanov then went on to explain how Russia could better defend its aircraft on the ground.

 chat, the results tray keeps its space reserved. */

 /* Leonardo's panel: the button and its verified line read as one block,

 .lh-heroalt-panel{border:1px solid #C3C9CE;border-radius:6px;background:#fff;overflow:hidden}
 .lh-heroalt-panel:hover{border-color:#E0742B}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo{border:0;border-radius:0;background:none;padding:15px 16px 13px}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo:hover,.lh-heroalt-card--leo:focus-visible{background:#FFFDFB;border:0}
 .lh-heroalt-kicker{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.2px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#12233D;font-weight:500}
 .lh-heroalt-kicker svg{color:#E0742B;flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-heroalt-card--leo .lh-heroalt-hint{margin-top:7px;font-size:13.5px;color:#3C4F66}
 .lh-heroalt-verified{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:flex-start;margin:0;padding:11px 16px 13px;border-top:1px solid #EDEAE3;background:#FBF8F2;font-size:12.5px;line-height:1.5;color:#4A525C}
 .lh-heroalt-verified svg{color:#1C7A4A;flex:0 0 auto;margin-top:2px}
 /* ── Make the search the priority, not an afterthought ────────────────
 Measured before this change at 1440x900: hero 1028px tall, search bar
 top at y=694. Tightened the vertical rhythm and moved the trust row
 below, which lifts the bar roughly 230px — comfortably in view. */
 .lh-hero.lh-hero{padding:clamp(28px,4vw,56px) 0 clamp(32px,4.5vw,64px)}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{gap:clamp(16px,2vw,26px)}
 /* ⚠️ THE CAUSE OF THE BIG EMPTY GAP, and it was mine. The stylesheet sets
 .lh-hero-text{flex:1 1 380px} and .lh-portals{flex:1 1 420px}. Those were
 written for the original ROW layout, where flex-basis is a WIDTH. Turning
 the container into a column silently turned both into fixed HEIGHTS: the
 text box stayed 380px tall although its content ended after 187px, and
 the search row stayed 420px tall although the cards are 195px. That is
 ~420px of enforced emptiness. Resetting the basis is the whole fix —
 never set flex-direction on an inherited flex container without checking
 what flex-basis meant before. */
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{flex:0 0 auto}
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{margin-bottom:10px}
 .lh-hero .lh-title{margin:0 0 12px}
 .lh-hero .lh-subtitle{margin:0;max-width:52ch}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{position:relative;z-index:1;margin:clamp(14px,1.8vw,22px) 0 0;gap:10px 24px}
 /* The bar itself carries the emphasis: taller, larger type, and a navy
 action instead of the yellow one — yellow reads promotional, and on warm
 paper it was the loudest thing in the hero. Scoped to .lh-herosearch so
 the same widget elsewhere keeps the brand button. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-bar{min-height:64px;padding:4px 6px 4px 14px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-input{font-size:17px}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn{background:#12233D;border-color:#12233D;color:#fff;font-weight:600}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-btn:hover{background:#1E3354;border-color:#1E3354}
 /* ── Results as a responsive grid, not a single strip ──────────────────
 .sie-res-list holds the program cards as direct children (verified live:
 18 cards, one parent, no headers in between), so one grid rule is enough.
 ⚠️ SCOPED TO THE HOMEPAGE ON PURPOSE. .sie-res-list is the shared
 SieFlowView markup — Leonardo renders into it too, with its own
 per-card animation offsets. Re-layouting it globally would change his
 results as a side effect of a homepage fix. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(320px,1fr));gap:16px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}
 /* The flow view (AI matching on) groups results into one .sie-flow__branch
 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.
 The first keeps padding-left:0 so its numeral lines up with the margin
 the hero headline uses. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-num{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(27px,2.9vw,40px);font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;line-height:1.05;color:#12233D;background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}
 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}
 @media(max-width:700px){
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr))}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:nth-child(2){border-right:0}
 }
 /* Monogram instead of a repeated building glyph. Hairline tile, serif
 letters — it reads as a placeholder somebody chose, not as missing data. */
 .lh-uni-logo-placeholder{display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;background:#F4F2ED;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:5px;color:#8A8578}
 .lh-uni-monogram{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:22px;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:1px;color:#12233D}
 /* ── For institutions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
 The one full navy band on the page. It is dark on purpose: it marks a
 change of audience, so a student scrolling past knows at a glance that
 this part is not addressed to them. */
 .lh-inst{background:#12233D;color:#fff}
 .lh-inst-wrap *,.lh-inst-wrap *::before,.lh-inst-wrap *::after{box-sizing:border-box}
 .lh-inst-inner{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:clamp(48px,6vw,88px) clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.35fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:clamp(28px,4vw,64px);align-items:start}
 .lh-inst-badge{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-h{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(26px,3.1vw,40px);line-height:1.16;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;color:#fff;max-width:20ch}
 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}
 .lh-inst-actions{margin:0;display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px}
 .lh-inst-btn{display:inline-block;text-decoration:none;background:#fff;color:#12233D;font-size:15.5px;font-weight:600;padding:14px 26px;border:1px solid #fff;border-radius:4px;min-height:44px}
 .lh-inst-btn:hover{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#44597A;font-weight:500}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost:hover{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-terms{margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none}
 .lh-inst-terms li{border-top:1px solid #28405F;padding:20px 0}
 .lh-inst-terms li:first-child{border-top:0;padding-top:0}
 .lh-inst-k{margin:0 0 6px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:19px;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-v{margin:0;font-size:15px;line-height:1.6;color:#C6D2E0}
 @media(max-width:860px){
 .lh-inst-inner{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 }
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-heroalt{flex-direction:row;flex-wrap:wrap}
 .lh-heroalt-card{flex:1 1 220px}
 .lh-hero-scrim{background:linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(250,248,244,.97) 0%,rgba(250,248,244,.93) 62%,rgba(250,248,244,.72) 100%)}
 }
 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
 /* The accent word: italic navy reads editorial; bright orange read promo. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-gradient-text{color:#12233D;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D;font-style:italic;font-weight:600}
 /* One label above the headline is enough. The H1 eyebrow ("STUDY IN
 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}
 /* Phones: the hero had no side gutter, so the eyebrow sat flush against
 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text,.lh-hero .lh-subtitle{text-align:left}
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 }
 /* ── Section headers: same voice as the institutions band ─────────────
 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-header h2{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px) !important;letter-spacing:-.4px;line-height:1.15;color:#12233D !important}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-how{background:#FAF8F4}
 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 /* How it works: the three steps were top-aligned, so the middle card
 (longer text) hung lower than its neighbours. Stretch evens them. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-steps{align-items:stretch}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step{background:#fff;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-num{background:#12233D;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-weight:500}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-icon{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D;border-radius:6px}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-arrow{color:#B7B1A5}
 /* Cards: tighter corners and hairlines everywhere. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card{border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px;border-color:#E4E0D8;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it
 the loudest part of the page. Same content, one navy, warm neutrals.
 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__source-pill{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;box-shadow:none !important;border-radius:4px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch{--branch-color:#12233D !important;--branch-bg:#F4F2ED !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-accent{display:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-icon{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card{background:#FAF8F4;border:1px solid #EDEAE3;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card:hover{border-color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel
 (blue / yellow / blue) via !important rules at .lh-uni-card:nth-child()
 specificity, so this needs one more class to win. Plain paper, so the
 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}
 /* Europe silhouette on the navy side. Present, never loud: a lighter blue
 at 15% so the copy on top keeps full contrast. The right edge fades out
 because the map is cut through Russia there, and a hard vertical cut
 would read as a mistake. The stroke in the fill colour closes the
 hairline seams between neighbouring countries; opacity sits on the <svg> itself so overlapping strokes cannot add up into darker lines. */
 .lh-hero-navy{overflow:hidden}
 .lh-hero-map{position:absolute;top:6%;bottom:6%;left:6%;width:92%;height:88%;opacity:.15;pointer-events:none;-webkit-mask-image:linear-gradient(to right,#000 78%,transparent 100%);mask-image:linear-gradient(to right,#000 78%,transparent 100%)}

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {

 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;

 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {

 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }

 body.sie-dest-panel-open {

 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);

 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);

 justify-content: center;

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
